chapters.title: 10 builds, one accountable model
chapters.promise: Creator geometry. Forge details. Assembly Line economics.
chapters.narration: This is the master tour of ten real Dome Creator builds. Every shell is rebuilt from the preset the walkable tool actually loads. The Dome Forge explains how the frame, panels, drains and water layers go together. The Assembly Line supplies the wage, overhead, labor ledger and product-family margin. The engine rendering this film keeps every number tied to those sources. For each build we will show the material breakdown, the labor-time breakdown, and a modeled direct-sale price. It is a planning model, not a contractor quote.

chapters.title: One codebase, five worlds
chapters.promise: Every tool computes from the same geometry.
chapters.narration: The project is one codebase wearing five faces. A dome creator you walk around in. A dome forge that builds one dome out of layers, like a paint program builds an image. A factory simulation that prices every screw. A teaching-video engine, which is what is rendering this very film. And a presenter studio that turns a script into a movie. They all read the same geometry module, so a strut length in one tool cannot disagree with the same strut in another.

chapters.title: The Dome Creator
chapters.promise: A build-a-home world with a live bill of materials.
chapters.narration: The Dome Creator is a walkable site. Click the ground and the avatar walks there. Click a panel and you can swap it: glass, shingle, solar, plastic sheeting, anything. Change the frequency, the radius, the frame material, the foundation. Every choice updates a live bill of materials: strut cut lists, panel weights, costs, even how many trees you would have to harvest. A camera hangs from every apex, watching the floor, counting what it sees. It is a sales floor, a design desk and a planning meeting in one window.

chapters.title: The Dome Forge
chapters.promise: One dome, made of layers you can peel apart.
chapters.narration: The Dome Forge is a single dome, taken apart like layers in a paint program. Frame, panels, drains, veins, ring, pipe, tank, rain -- every part is its own layer you can hide, fade, reorder or tune. The default stack answers the oldest dome complaint there is. Domes leak, people say. So the panels dish inward and drain to one point each. A vein runs along the inside of every seam, standing off from the skin, so anything that gets past a joint lands in a channel instead of your floor. The veins run downhill to a collector ring, down a pipe, into a cistern. The leak becomes the water supply.

chapters.title: The Assembly Line
chapters.promise: Fifteen stations, and every dollar accounted for.
chapters.narration: The assembly line is a factory simulation in the real trailer-plant order. A carriage rolls the home down the rails through fifteen stations: floor, frame, utility column, water, power, fixtures, insulation, sheetrock, sheathing, membrane, shingle scales, fiberglass, the sealed hatch, the fit-out, the solar band. Every element carries a real material cost and a real install time, and a simulated crew walks every part from the stockpile at a human stride, so the labor hours are earned, not assumed. Panels show profit and loss, the bottleneck station, break-even. It is an investor tool that happens to look like a video game.

chapters.title: The engine rendering this film
chapters.promise: Programmatic video: correct because it is computed.
chapters.narration: And the film you are watching right now is the fifth tool. Every frame is a pure function of time. Every scene is drawn by code, and every figure on screen is calculated by a module that also proves itself before a single frame renders. Generative video cannot be asked to be correct. This can. That promise is about to matter, because of what comes next.

chapters.title: Timber Workshop
chapters.promise: The default: a working shop you can actually afford to frame.
chapters.narration: The one the tool opens on. Three frequency, five metre radius, dimensional lumber on metal brackets, plywood skin, concrete slab. It is a workshop: assembly bay, two wood shop wedges, a metal shop, storage and an office, with the benches and machines already placed. If you want to know what a dome costs as a building rather than as an idea, this is the honest starting point. The cost stack on screen is the model, not a bid. The amber line splits the Creator bill of materials into frame, enclosure, foundation and fit-out. The purple line totals 96 labor hours from the Creator's own construction events, separated into site, frame, enclosure, and systems work. The green line then applies the Assembly Line wage, overhead, and its shed product-family margin to produce the modeled direct-sale price.

chapters.narration: Here is that trade as arithmetic, off both real models. The hubless frame carries nearly twice the sticks. In exchange it needs exactly zero hub connectors, which is the part you would otherwise have to weld, buy or wait for. And because its struts are quarter wedges split from logs, the model even reports the trees, at four wedges to a log.
equations: both are 2V domes from this world:
Whole Trunk Lodge - 20 ft  --  Hub & Strut
struts 65,  hubs 26,  bolts 0
Split-Log Homestead  --  Hubless Doubled
struts 120,  hubs 0,  bolts 130
the hubless frame carries 1.8x the sticks
and exactly 0 hub connectors
every triangle brings its own three boards, so each shared
seam ends up two boards thick and bolts to its neighbour
and because its struts are split logs, the model reports 30 trees to harvest at 4 wedges a log
you trade wood for hardware: more sticks, zero hubs, and nothing on the critical path you cannot cut yourself

chapters.title: The cheapest wall is the one you never build
chapters.promise: Envelope per square foot of floor, ranked.
chapters.narration: One more comparison, and it is the one the whole shape is for. For every square foot of floor, how many square feet of outside do you have to build, seal, insulate and heat? Lower is better, and the spread here is set by the geometry, not by what is bolted to it.

chapters.title: Envelope per floor, measured
chapters.promise: Geometry decides this one, not materials.
chapters.narration: The best and worst designs in the catalogue differ by a wide margin on this measure, and every one of them is a dome. The driver is frequency and where the shell gets cut, which is the same parity effect you saw on the gold line. It is worth knowing before you choose a frequency, because this number follows you for the whole life of the building.

chapters.title: Size is a number you type
chapters.promise: The same parts list at three different sizes.
chapters.narration: And here is why this is a product rather than a craft. These three designs are all two frequency, so all three have exactly sixty-five struts and forty panels. The smallest is a twenty- eight foot treehouse dome. The largest is a sixty-five foot lodge with five and a half times the floor. The sticks get longer. The list of operations does not change at all.

chapters.title: Scale, proved on the catalogue
chapters.promise: More house for the same list of operations.
chapters.narration: Part counts depend on frequency alone. Never on size. So the largest dome in this world has several times the floor of the smallest, off an identical set of repeated operations. That is the entire economic argument for this shape, and you can check it yourself in the tool in about a minute: load a preset, change the radius slider, and watch the part counts stay exactly where they were.

chapters.title: What the model refuses to hide
chapters.promise: Curves, code, freight, site work, and local engineering still exist.
chapters.narration: A dome does not make the difficult parts of housing disappear. Curved walls complicate ordinary cabinets and openings. Unfamiliar systems can slow permits, insurance and appraisal. Freight and site work can dominate a remote job. Every occupied structure still needs local structural engineering and code review. Those costs are not secretly folded into the green number. They are outside it, stated here on purpose. What this model can defend is the geometry, the generated bill of materials, the construction-event hours, and the exact conversion rule used to reach the planning price.

chapters.title: Open the tools and audit the film
chapters.promise: Every dome, dollar, and labor hour has a path back to code.
chapters.narration: That is the master cut: ten finished configurations from the Dome Creator, the layer logic of the Dome Forge, the production ledger of the Assembly Line, and the deterministic engine that turned all of it into a film. The report beside the video lists every material bucket, every labor phase, every conversion cost and every modeled direct-sale price. Open the tools, change a preset, and run it again. The point is not that you have to trust this video. The point is that you do not.

chapters.title: Do the one thing
chapters.promise: Send this to one person who can carry it further than I can.
chapters.narration: If any of this was worth your time, send it to one person who can carry it further than I can. That is the whole ask. One share from somebody with reach does more for this than a month of me in a field with a chainsaw.

title: Why Wedges: A Dome That Does Not Need a Sawmill
note: The combined cut. Where the method came from (the frankendome and its V brackets), what it is (borrowing the mechanism chapters and three math screens from `wedge` so the two films cannot disagree), and what it is worth -- from two timed cutting sessions that agree with a geometric prediction to 12%, a wedge valued two independent ways that land 1% apart, the store-bought overheads nobody counts, and a structural claim stated as a crossover diameter rather than a verdict.

chapters.title: Why I build like this
chapters.promise: The tree is already the right shape for something.
chapters.narration: Every stick of framing lumber you can buy started as a round, tapered, slightly bent thing, and was then cut, edged, dried, planed and graded until it became a rectangle. That rectangle is not a structural requirement. It is a handling requirement. Rectangles stack on a pallet, price by the piece and fit a stud wall. A geodesic dome does not need any of that. It needs sticks whose ends can be made to meet. So I stopped making rectangles. This is how that decision got made, what it does, and what it is worth, in numbers I measured rather than adjectives I chose.
equations: 120 members from split logs
40 panels, one flat jig

chapters.title: It started with the frankendome
chapters.promise: A shell that did not care what shape its sticks were.
chapters.narration: Before any of this there was the frankendome. Forty triangles joined along their edges from the top down, and deliberately strut-agnostic: any section, any stock, whatever was to hand. The crown was the interesting part. Instead of the usual fifteen-piece pentagon it used one strut from each corner to the apex rather than two, making a heavier-duty ten-piece cap. What that build proved is the thing everything after it depends on. If the shell will accept members of any section, then the section stops being a constraint and becomes a choice.
equations: 40 triangles, joined edge to edge
10-piece crown pentagon, not 15

chapters.title: The V bracket that made it possible
chapters.promise: One connector that does not care what it is holding.
chapters.narration: Edge-to-edge joining between odd-shaped members is a bracket problem, and most bracket types need to know what they are gripping before you can make them. A V bracket does not. It folds to the corner angle and seats inside the vee between two struts, with long legs running down each one and the screws spread wide along that length. The spread is what stops the joint rotating, and because the bracket only ever touches the inside faces it does not care what section it has hold of. That is exactly why the frankendome used it. I wanted to study how different trunk-harvested strut types behaved against each other, and this connector let me mix them freely. It also scales by repetition. Need more corner? Add another, longer bracket over the first. I built it that way knowing I could keep stacking them as the domes got bigger.
equations: folded from flat stock
any member type, same corner

chapters.title: What holds the wedge dome together
chapters.promise: Not brackets. These members are all alike, so the joint gets simpler.
chapters.narration: The V bracket solves a problem the wedge build does not have. It exists to join unlike things, and every member here is the same shape as every other one. So the joint gets to be simpler. Inside a triangle the members are glued on their mating faces and screwed in from the far side of the neighbour, so the fastening pulls the joint together rather than hanging off it. Between triangles, the panels bolt to each other edge to edge, and the bolt can pass straight through one of the seam keys that was going in anyway. If I do end up wanting brackets on a wedge dome, they will have to change shape to suit it. The frankendome's are the wrong tool for a frame this uniform.
equations: glued faces, screws from the neighbour's side
panels bolted edge to edge through a key

chapters.title: What a mill is actually for
chapters.promise: Four machines whose entire job is making a circle into a box.
chapters.narration: A sawmill breaks the log down. An edger squares the waney sides. A trimmer squares the ends. A planing mill, usually a separate plant altogether, surfaces four faces to a known dimension. None of those machines make the wood stronger. Every one of them exists to make a round, tapered, irregular thing into a rectangular prism that can be stacked, priced and shipped. That is a genuinely useful thing to do if you are building a stud wall. It is a completely wasted effort if you are building a shell out of triangles.
equations: square, edge, trim, plane
none of it adds strength

chapters.title: The corners of a round log
chapters.promise: Waste is not bad wood. It is wood of the wrong shape.
chapters.narration: Put a rectangle inside a circle and you leave four crescents outside it. Put a second rectangle beside the first and the crescents get bigger, because the circle is pinching in. None of that discarded wood is defective. It is slabs and edgings and planer shavings because it failed a geometry test, not a strength test. Split the same section radially instead and there are no crescents at all. Every sector runs from the pith to the bark, and the only wood that leaves is the width of the saw.
equations: radial split: pith to bark, no offcut
sawn: everything outside the rectangle

chapters.title: How much of the tree survives
chapters.promise: The same two trees, converted both ways, counted in board feet.
chapters.narration: This is one pine measured at the butt and at the top, bucked into twelve foot sections, and then converted twice on paper. Split radially it keeps almost everything, losing only the kerf of the passes down each section. Packed with rectangles it keeps under half, and that is with the rectangles packed as favourably as a mill would pack them. The measured figure across whole trees on site is eighty-eight percent, against fifty to sixty-five for square milling, which loses wood to a good deal more than the kerf.
equations: one trunk: 15.0 in at the butt, 5.5 in at the top, 60 ft usable
bucked into 5 sections of 12 ft
solid wood in those sections = 442.1 board feet
SPLIT RADIALLY:
8 sectors per section, 45 deg each = 40 full-length sectors from one tree
the saw passes remove 51.2 bf of kerf
measured across whole trees on site: 88 %
SAWN INTO TRUE TWO-BY-FOURS, same sections:
rectangles that grid-pack inside the round = 25 pieces
square milling in practice recovers 50-65 %, losing wood to slabs, edgings, trim, drying degrade and planer shavings
crosscut once, one tree gives 80 members; the dome needs 120 and 2 trees give 160
The same two trees yield 1.95 times as much usable structure split as sawn, because a wedge is not trying to be a rectangle and so throws none of the round away.

chapters.title: Three cuts and it is structure
chapters.promise: One saw, one sequence, and the stick exists.
chapters.narration: The whole conversion is one saw and a sequence. Halve the round. Halve each half. Halve each quarter. Eight sectors, forty-five degrees each, and every one of them already has two flat faces and a curved back. Nothing is squared, nothing is edged, nothing is dried to a spec and nothing is planed. The sawn faces come off the split flat enough to bear on each other, which is the only flatness this building needs.
equations: 8 sectors, 45 deg each
two sawn faces, one bark back

chapters.title: One eighth of a tree, used as a stick
chapters.promise: The section is a wedge, and the wedge is the point.
chapters.narration: A member here is literally an eighth of the trunk. It keeps the pith line as a sharp edge, the two radial saw cuts as flat faces, and the outer growth rings as a curved back. Put the bark face outward and the densest wood in the tree ends up on the weather side, while the deep dimension of the section faces the load. How strong that is depends on how big the tree was, and that turns out to be the hinge the whole structural argument swings on. We will come back to it with a number.
equations: bark out, pith in
1/8 of the trunk, per member

chapters.title: The member, measured
chapters.promise: What one raw sector is, in section and in bearing.
chapters.narration: This is the member the rest of the film keeps referring to, measured rather than described: the sector's angle, its chord and depth, the area it presents, and what that is worth against a two-by-four. The bearing figure matters more than it looks. In this frame one member's end presses on the flat sawn side of the next, so the joint's capacity is an area of wood against wood rather than a fastener in shear.
equations: one sector is 45 degrees of the round:
area  = pi r^2 / 8
width = 2 r sin(180 deg / 8)   across the bark face
depth = r                      pith to bark
at the design diameter of 12.5 in:
area  = 15.34 sq in
width = 4.78 in
depth = 6.25 in
a true 2x4 is 2 x 4 = 8 sq in, so this
sector is worth 1.92 of them
and the depth is the useful part: bending stiffness grows with
the cube of depth, and this section is deep and narrow
the break-even diameter, where one eighth equals one 2x4:
pi r^2 / 8 = 8  ->  diameter = 9.03 in
check: sector at 9.0 in = 8.00 sq in
Above about 9 inches of trunk, every eighth of the log already holds more wood than a two-by-four -- before any milling at all.

chapters.title: Why six feet is the useful length
chapters.promise: A defect in a long stick ruins a long stick.
chapters.narration: The members here are short, and that is not a compromise. A knot or a bend does not destroy wood; it destroys whatever length has to be thrown away around it. That length is set by the piece you were trying to make. On a sixteen foot stick, one bad metre in the middle costs the whole board. On six foot pieces it costs one piece. It also means a crooked farm tree is usable. Cut the bend out at its middle, go six feet clear either side, and the sections above and below it are both still structure.
equations: short pieces, more places for a defect to fall
a bend costs one piece, not one board

chapters.title: What one bend actually costs
chapters.promise: The same flaw, priced against two different piece lengths.
chapters.narration: Here is the arithmetic behind that. A single defect takes out one piece, so its cost as a share of the tree is just the length of the piece you were cutting. Short members make a defect several times cheaper, and they also give the trunk more pieces, so there are more places for a flaw to fall harmlessly between two of them. In square milling the same bend follows the board down its whole length, because the rectangle has to be straight before it exists at all.
equations: a knot or a bend does not ruin wood. It ruins whatever length has
to be thrown away around it -- and that length is the piece you
were trying to make.
this dome's members run 5.13 to 5.90 ft, cut from 6 ft stock
a 16 ft stick from the same trunk is 2.7 times longer
one defect costs, out of 60 usable ft:
short members  6 ft = 10.0 % of the tree
long sticks   16 ft = 26.7 % of the tree
and the trunk gives 10 short pieces against 3 long ones, so there are more places for a
defect to fall harmlessly between
a real bend is cut out at its middle: go six feet clear either side
and the sections above and below it are both still good
in square milling the same bend follows the board down its whole
length, because the rectangle has to be straight before it exists
Short modular members make a defect 2.7 times cheaper, which is what lets a crooked farm tree be structure instead of firewood.

chapters.title: This is the actual solved shell
chapters.promise: Not a drawing of the dome. The dome.
chapters.narration: Everything you are about to see about frames, joints and seams comes out of one solver, and this is its output rather than an artist's impression of it. A hundred and twenty members, each with its own compound butt cut, its own clean vertex trim and its own place in a pinwheel. Fifty-five interior seams, each with the key that closes it. When a number appears on screen later in this film, it was measured off this, not typed in beside it.
equations: 120 members, 55 seams
rendered from the solver itself

chapters.title: Forty frames, not one lattice
chapters.promise: Each triangle is finished before it meets its neighbours.
chapters.narration: The shell is not assembled stick by stick in the air. It is forty independent triangular frames, each one completed flat on a bench and then lifted into place. That is what turns a geodesic dome from a scaffolding problem into a panel problem. The awkward geometry all happens on a board at waist height, indoors, in daylight. It also means a panel can be rejected, remade or replaced without touching anything else.
equations: 40 independent frames
every joint made flat on a bench

chapters.title: The joint with no mitres in it
chapters.promise: No mitres, no coping, nothing shaved to a point.
chapters.narration: Inside each triangle the three members run as a same-handed pinwheel. Every member's end lands on the flat side of the next one, the same way round for all three. What that removes is the shared vertex. No two ends ever meet each other, nothing is coped, and no stick is shaved to a point. The mathematical corner becomes a reference that no member reaches. What it does not remove is the cut. Every butt still has to be shaped to land flat on the side of the next member, and that side is tilted two ways at once. I have said elsewhere that this frame has no mitres in it. That was wrong, and the next chapter is the correction.
equations: end to side, three times round
no shared vertex -- but the butt is still a compound cut

chapters.title: The pinwheel, measured
chapters.promise: Offsets, bearing and the gap at the mathematical vertex.
chapters.narration: The pinwheel is not free. Every member sits a small distance back from the ideal edge, and that offset is what opens the gap at the vertex that no stick reaches. Both figures come out of the same solve, and they are what the jig later has to hold. The bearing area is the joint's real capacity; the vertex gap is what has to be trimmed away cleanly so that panels do not fight each other at a node.
equations: three members, one triangle, and not a single mitre:
each member lies with its bark face on its own edge line
so its centre sits 2.39 in inside that line -- half its width
each end is a square crosscut, and the two ends do different
jobs, the same way round for all three members:
the HEAD is cut against the side of the next member
the TAIL runs on through the previous member's band, so that
member's head has a full face to bear on
bearing length = 5.129 in of contact
the corner is where the two bands cross, so no wood reaches it:
nearest end to the mathematical vertex = 3.134 in
which is why the triangle's corners are references, not
endpoints -- the geometry is exact even though no stick is
cut to it
the price is that the sticks are shorter than their edges:
edge 72.146 in, member 62.523 in, inset 9.623 in
Every end in the whole frame is a square crosscut: the pinwheel trades a little length for the hardest operation in dome building disappearing entirely.

chapters.title: The cut I said did not exist
chapters.promise: The trickiest operation in the build, and I skipped past it.
chapters.narration: In an earlier version of this film I said nothing in this frame is mitred. That is not true, and it is the sort of error that makes somebody trust a method and then be ambushed by it at the bench. Every butt end has to be shaped to sit flat on the sloped side of the member it lands on. That means an angle across the stick and an angle through it, at once. It is a compound cut, it is the hardest thing in the build, and without a fixture it is gauged by eye. The cut also runs a long way down the member, because the face it lands on is itself leaning away. The sector's point has to reach further than its bark corner, so the blank is long on the point side and the saw is walked up from the short one.
equations: bevel 22.50 deg on every member
3 mitre settings in the whole shell

chapters.title: How many settings it really takes
chapters.promise: The correction, and then the number that rescues it.
chapters.narration: Here is the compound cut, solved rather than described. Two things fall out of it that turn gauging by hand into a fixture. The bevel is identical on every member in the dome, and it is exactly half the sector angle. It is set by how the log was split, not by where the member sits in the shell, so you set it once and never touch it again. And the mitre takes only three values across all hundred and twenty members, all of them inside the swing of a common saw. So the cradle holds one sawn face down with the point against a fence, the bevel stays locked, and there are three stops.
equations: correction first. An earlier cut of this film said nothing in this
frame is mitred. That is wrong, and it is the most important
thing on this screen.
the PINWHEEL removes the shared vertex: no two ends ever meet each
other, nothing is coped, nothing is shaved to a point.
but every butt end still lands on the SIDE of the next member, and
that side is tilted two ways at once -- by the sector angle, and
by the turn the member makes to close the triangle.
so the butt is a compound cut, and it is the hardest operation in
the build. Here is what the solve says it costs:
BEVEL 22.500 deg on every one of 120 members
and 22.500 = half the sector angle (22.500), set by the SPLIT, not by the dome
MITRE takes 3 values in the whole shell:
34.431 deg   x 60 members
21.138 deg   x 30 members
30.000 deg   x 30 members
largest is 34.431 deg, inside a common saw's 50 deg swing
the cut runs 2.23 to 2.91 in along the member, because it lands on a slope:
the sector's POINT reaches furthest and the bark corner least, so
the blank has to be long on the point side and the cut is walked from the short corner up
One bevel, locked at 22.5 degrees and never touched, and 3 mitre stops. That is what turns the hardest cut in the build from gauging by hand into a fixture.

chapters.title: Neighbours never share a stick
chapters.promise: Two members along every shared edge, on purpose.
chapters.narration: A conventional frame would put one member on the edge between two panels and bolt both to it. This one does not. Each panel carries its own member along that edge, so the shell has two. That sounds wasteful and is the opposite. It means a panel is complete before it meets anything, and it means the joint between panels is a connection between two finished things rather than a shared dependency. It also doubles the wood on every interior edge, which is where the structural argument later gets its margin from.
equations: 55 interior seams, two members each
panels finish before they meet

The second pile is estimated, and every item in it sits on the store-bought side of the comparison. That is the side it flatters me least to be guessing about.

chapters.title: Machines that stop being necessary
chapters.promise: Each conversion step is a building full of steel somebody owns.
chapters.narration: Follow a log through the conversion chain and count the plant. A headrig, an edger, a trimmer, a kiln, a grading line and a planing mill, which is usually a separate factory again. The wedge path keeps the chainsaw that felled the tree and drops the rest, because a split face is already flat, already exact, and already dry enough for a shell that is not a graded-lumber assembly. I started this build believing it saved me one entire mill. The count says more than that, and the count is on the next screen rather than the claim.
equations: SAWMILL, EDGER, PLANING MILL
the chainsaw does the primary breakdown

chapters.title: Counting the machines out
chapters.promise: Station by station, which survives and which does not.
chapters.narration: Here is the whole chain with the wedge path laid alongside it. Felling and bucking is in both, so it cancels. Crosscutting to length is in both. End joinery is in both too, though it is a very different operation on each side, and that difference is most of the time saving later. What is left on the wedge side, at the end of the count, is one chainsaw and a flat board.
equations: what has to happen to a log before it can hold a roof up:
BOTH  fell and buck            chainsaw
identical in both, so it cancels
SAWN  primary breakdown        SAWMILL
wedge path splits radially with the same chainsaw
SAWN  edging                   EDGER
there is no waney edge to remove from a split face
SAWN  drying and grading       kiln / grader
wedges are used green; the shell is not a graded-lumber assembly
SAWN  surfacing to dimension   PLANING MILL
the sawn faces come off the split already flat and already exact
BOTH  crosscut to length       crosscut saw
one square cut, both paths
BOTH  end joinery              compound saw / jig
sawn path measures two compound ends; wedge path cuts one butt and flush-cuts the head in place
machines the wedge path never buys, feeds or houses: 3
SAWMILL, EDGER, PLANING MILL
what is left on the wedge side is one chainsaw and a flat board
The dome removes 3 whole machines from the chain, and it can only do that because a triangulated shell does not care whether its sticks are rectangular.

chapters.title: What a shelf price is made of
chapters.promise: Almost none of it is the tree.
chapters.narration: When you buy a stud you are not mostly buying wood. You are buying the sawing, the drying, the planing, the grading, the log truck, the flatbed, the warehouse that held it and the yard that sold it. None of those people are villains and none of that work is fake. But every one of those steps exists to turn a round local thing into a standard shippable thing. A dome does not need it to be standard, and I do not need it to be shipped, because the tree was already here.
equations: 15 hands between the tree and the rack
$8.88 on the rack, $10.00 paid

chapters.title: Fifteen sets of hands
chapters.promise: Listed, because a round number is easy to say and hard to check.
chapters.narration: Claiming you have cut out about fifteen middle men is the sort of thing that deserves a list rather than a wave, so here is the list. Every one of them took a margin, and every one of those margins is in the price on the rack, along with the tax on top of all of it. The wedge path in full is three steps: fell the tree, rip the trunk, use the wood.
equations: a stud on a rack has been sold and handled this many times:
1. timber broker        sells the standing timber
2. logging contractor   fells and skids it
3. log haulier          trucks it to the mill yard
4. log scaler           measures and grades the log
5. headrig sawyer       breaks the log down
6. edger operator       squares the waney sides
7. trimmer operator     squares the ends
8. kiln operator        dries it to a moisture spec
9. lumber grader        stamps a grade on it
10. planing mill         surfaces four sides to dimension
11. bundler              packs and wraps a unit
12. mill sales           sells the unit
13. freight broker       books the flatbed
14. distributor          holds stock and breaks bulk
15. retail yard          sells you one stick
then sales tax: $8.88 on the rack becomes $10.00 paid
every one of the 15 took a margin, and every margin is in that price
the wedge path is: fell the tree, rip the trunk, use the wood
Cutting your own wedges removes 15 separate parties from between the tree and the wall, none of whom did anything to the wood that a geodesic shell needed done.

chapters.title: What the saw actually does
chapters.promise: Two sittings, timed, with the fuel written down.
chapters.narration: Everything so far could be argued. This part was measured. One sitting produced twelve wedges in two hours and burned ten dollars of fuel and bar oil. A separate sitting cut forty-two feet of rip at six inches of depth in one hour, on two tanks of fuel and two of bar oil, including a chain sharpening. Those two sessions counted different things, which is what makes them worth having. Divide one by the other and you get feet of cut per finished wedge, and the geometry can predict that number independently.
equations: 6 wedges/hour
42 ft of rip/hour

chapters.title: Do the two sessions agree?
chapters.promise: A prediction the geometry can make without being told.
chapters.narration: Splitting a round into eight sectors takes seven passes down the whole length of the section. That is a pure geometric statement and it gives feet of cut per wedge without any timing at all. Set it beside the number the two timed sessions imply and they land close. The gap between them is rolling the log, setting up and sharpening, which is exactly the sort of thing that should be the difference. Planning then uses a rate below both, because an afternoon is not a timed sprint.
equations: SESSION A, timed:
12 wedges in 2.0 h = 6.0 wedges/hour
$10.00 of fuel and bar oil = $5.00/hour, the only cash spent
SESSION B, timed separately:
6 passes at 7 ft = 42 ft of rip in 1 h, at 6 in+ of depth
2 tanks of fuel and 2 of bar oil, one sharpening
the two sessions measured different things, so divide them:
42 ft/h / 6.0 wedges/h = 7.00 ft of rip per wedge
and the geometry predicts the same number independently:
8 sectors takes 7 passes down a 7 ft section
7 x 7 / 8 = 6.12 ft per wedge
the pure cutting is 88 % of the measured time; the other 12 % is rolling the log, setting up and sharpening
planning uses 5.0 wedges/hour, 17 % below the measured rate
Two independent measurements and a geometric prediction agree to within 12 percent, which is why the rate below is worth anything at all.

chapters.title: What one wedge is worth
chapters.promise: Priced against the sticks it would take to replace it.
chapters.narration: A wedge is not one two-by-four. It is thicker, so comparing them piece for piece would quietly build a weaker dome and call it cheaper. The honest comparison is by cross-section: how many dressed studs you would have to lay alongside one wedge to match the wood in it. At the trunk diameter I actually cut, that number is close to three, and the estimate I have been using for planning is two.
equations: 2.69 studs' section per wedge
$10.00 of wood per wedge

chapters.title: The rule of thumb, checked
chapters.promise: Two ways to price a wedge, and how far apart they land.
chapters.narration: The rule of thumb multiplies a conservative section factor by the price of an eight-foot stud section. The strict version uses the computed section and also corrects for the fact that a six-foot wedge is shorter than an eight-foot stud. They should not agree as closely as they do. The conservative multiplier and the generous length happen to cancel almost exactly, which is a piece of luck rather than a method. Either way, an afternoon of ripping produces a specific number of dollars of wood I would otherwise have had to buy.
equations: a 2x4x16 untreated pine is $8.88 on the rack, $10.00 with tax
= $5.00 per eight-foot section
one 1/8 wedge of a 12 in trunk has 14.14 in2 of section
a dressed 2x4 has 5.25 in2
computed multiplier = 14.14 / 5.25 = 2.69 x
the estimate on site was 2.5 x
the multiplier actually used for planning was 2.0 x -- lower than both
RULE OF THUMB:
STRICT, counting section AND the length difference:
the two disagree by 1.0 %
at 5 wedges an hour that is $50.00/hour gross, $45.00 after fuel
one 6-hour afternoon: 30 wedges, $300 of wood, $30 of fuel
A conservative multiplier and a generous length cancel almost exactly, so both methods say the same thing: about $45 an hour, in wood you would otherwise have had to buy.

chapters.title: The part nobody counts
chapters.promise: Culls, trips, hours and the boards that never make it.
chapters.narration: A shelf price is not what lumber costs you. There is the drive there and back, the time picking through a rack for boards that are not bowed, the queue, the loading and the unloading. There are the boards you buy and then reject anyway, and the ones that split or soak between the yard and the site. You paid for those too. My chainsaw's fuel bill sits roughly where the truck's fuel bill would have been, so it is not the consumables that differ. It is everything attached to them.
equations: 10% bought and rejected
4 truck loads, 6.0 h of driving

chapters.title: The same frame, bought
chapters.promise: Enough studs to match the section, plus everything attached.
chapters.narration: This prices the store-bought route properly: enough dressed studs to match the cross-section the wedges provide, not one stud per member, because those are not the same building. Then the culls, the transit losses, the truck runs and the hours those runs take. Every one of those is an estimate and every one is on the side of the comparison I am arguing against. The cutting column is the measured rate and the measured fuel, and it contains no trips at all.
equations: to match the section 120 wedges provide you would need 2.69 dressed studs alongside each one
120 x 6 ft x 2.69 = 1939 stud-feet
/ 16 ft = 121 sticks of actual wood needed
then the part nobody counts:
10 % bought and rejected -- bowed, twisted, wet, split
3 % lost to handling and weather on the way
so you buy 139 sticks, 18 of which become firewood ($176)
4 truck loads x 40 mi = 160 mi at $0.55/mi = $88
and 6.0 h of driving, picking, queuing, loading and unloading = $150 of time
BOUGHT: $1476 cash, $1626 with the time
CUT: 24 h of ripping, $120 of fuel and oil, no trips at all
The chainsaw's fuel bill roughly replaces the truck's, so the real difference is $1356 of cash that never leaves, and a stack of wood that was already on the property.

chapters.title: The number that depends on the tree
chapters.promise: The one figure that could sink all of this.
chapters.narration: A raw sector is literally one eighth of the tree. Whether that is a stronger stick than a two-by-four is not a yes or a no; it is a question about diameter. Cross-section grows with the square of the radius and bending stiffness grows with the cube, so there is a trunk diameter where the sector overtakes the stud, and below it the sector loses. I am going to give you that crossover diameter rather than a slogan, because it is the one number that could sink this whole method and it deserves to be said out loud.
equations: crossover at 9.14 in of trunk
the trees being cut are 12-15 in

chapters.title: Section properties, and the crossover
chapters.promise: Area, second moment and section modulus, at both diameters.
chapters.narration: These are not looked up. The sector outline comes out of the same code that builds the dome, and the area and second moments are integrated around that polygon, checked against the closed form for a circular sector. At the eight-inch trunk the simulator defaults to, one wedge is the weaker stick in bending. At the twelve-inch trunks I actually cut, it is comfortably the stronger one. The crossover is solved for rather than asserted. None of this is an engineer's design check. A real build needs species, grade, moisture and somebody who will sign it. This is the geometry underneath that conversation.
equations: a raw sector is literally 1/8 of the tree, and how strong that is depends entirely on how big the tree was.
AT THE SIMULATOR'S 8 IN TRUNK:
area 6.28 in2, S 2.05 in3
= 120 % of a dressed 2x4's area but only 67 % of its bending
AT THE 12 IN TRUNKS ACTUALLY BEING CUT:
= 269 % of a dressed 2x4's area and 226 % of its bending
and 177 % / 130 % against a FULL-dimension 2x4
section grows with the square of the radius and bending with the
cube, so there is a diameter where the sector overtakes the stud:
more area than a dressed 2x4 above 7.31 in
stiffer than a dressed 2x4 above 9.14 in
stiffer than a FULL 2x4 above 11.00 in
and neighbouring panels never share a stick, so all 55 interior edges carry TWO sectors:
539 % of a stud's area, 452 % of its bending
Under 9.1 inches of trunk the wedge is the weaker member and this argument fails. The trees being cut are 12 to 15 inches, which is why it does not.

chapters.title: Four ways up, one of them free
chapters.promise: The wedge is not symmetric, so which way it faces is a decision.
chapters.narration: A sector has a point, two flat sawn faces and a curved bark back. Rotate it about its own long axis and you have four distinct positions in the wall. The way to read them is to look at a pair either side of one seam. The points can face into the dome together, out at the sky together, apart into their own panels, or in toward each other across the seam. It costs nothing to choose. Same stick, same wood, turned before it goes down. But the choice changes how deep the section is in the direction the shell actually bends.
equations: points in, points out, points apart, points together
same wood, different depth under load

chapters.title: A panel that cannot fall through
chapters.promise: Point the wedge outward and the opening tapers.
chapters.narration: Here is the part that made me stop thinking of these as struts and start thinking of them as a chassis. Turn every member so its pith faces out and its fat bark faces in. The opening in the middle of each triangle is now wider at the outside than the inside, because each member gets wider as it goes inward. A panel dropped in from outside seats on that taper and is physically stopped. It is a keystone. Which means a panel is not cladding. It is a swappable module. You want an air conditioner: you attach one to a panel and swap the panel. Shelving, glazing, a vent, a whole fitted appliance -- all of it becomes something you pop in and out.
equations: opening 1.53 in wider outside
panels become swappable modules

chapters.title: A vein through the whole shell
chapters.promise: The same rotation leaves a duct along every seam.
chapters.narration: That rotation does something else for free. With the points facing out, the two sawn faces either side of a seam open away from each other, and they leave a continuous V running the length of every seam in the dome. Every seam meets every other one at a vertex, so it is not a set of grooves. It is one connected network through the entire shell. Fill it with key and it is a joint. Leave some of it and it is a duct: air moved between outside and inside, water, wire, pipe, run anywhere on the building without cutting into anything structural.
equations: 7.3 in2 along 309 ft of seam
16 cu ft, all connected

chapters.title: Four rotations, four buildings
chapters.promise: Where the panel is caught, where the services run, what the saw does.
chapters.narration: Stiffness was one axis of this choice and it is already covered. Here are the others, measured off the same cross-section. Point out and a panel is caught from outside with the conduit in the weather. Point in and it is caught from inside with the services in the warm. Turn it sideways and the opening goes parallel: no lip, panels held by fixings, but the sawn faces come much closer to flat, which is what sheathing wants to land on. And one of the four does something I did not expect until the solve printed it. Turned sideways with the points facing each other across the seam, the butt cut's bevel goes to zero. The hardest cut in the build becomes a plain mitre.
equations: stiffness is one axis of the choice and it is already covered.
here is what each rotation does to the BUILDING:
DOME-IN
S  2.05 in3   depth 4.00 in   butt bevel +22.50 deg
lip -1.53 in -- panel goes in from INSIDE and cannot fall out
seam V 22.5-27.0 deg, 3.3 in2 -> 7.1 cu ft of continuous conduit
sawn faces sit 67.5 deg off the dome surface
PANEL-IN
S  1.63 in3   depth 3.06 in   butt bevel -67.50 deg
no lip: opening is parallel-sided, panels held by fixings
seam opens to 153-157 deg: a shallow dish, not a duct
sawn faces sit 22.5 deg off the dome surface
DOME-OUT
S  2.05 in3   depth 4.00 in   butt bevel -22.50 deg
lip +1.53 in -- panel drops in from OUTSIDE and cannot fall through
seam V 63.0-67.5 deg, 7.3 in2 -> 15.6 cu ft of continuous conduit
sawn faces sit 67.5 deg off the dome surface
PANEL-OUT
S  1.63 in3   depth 3.06 in   butt bevel  +0.00 deg
no lip: opening is parallel-sided, panels held by fixings
seam opens to 153-157 deg: a shallow dish, not a duct
sawn faces sit 22.5 deg off the dome surface
so: DOME-OUT catches a panel from OUTSIDE like a keystone, and puts 16 cu ft of conduit out there too
DOME-IN catches it from INSIDE and runs the services in the warm
PANEL-IN and PANEL-OUT present the flattest wood to sheathing, 22.5 deg off the surface
PANEL-OUT makes the hardest cut in the build a plain mitre, bevel 0.0 deg
Four rotations, four different buildings out of one stick: where the panel is caught, which side the services run, what sheathing lands on, and how hard the one difficult cut is.

chapters.title: What the rotation is worth
chapters.promise: The same area, turned four ways, measured each time.
chapters.narration: A shell member is pushed in and out along the dome's own radius, so the stiffness that matters is measured in that direction. Turn the sector and the area does not move by a thousandth of an inch, because rotating a shape does not add wood to it. The section modulus moves a great deal. Pointing the wedge at the centre of the dome, bark out at the weather, is the position that puts the most depth where the bending is. It also puts the densest outer wood on the wet side and leaves both flat sawn faces where the seam key wants them.
equations: the wedge is not symmetric, so which way it faces is a decision.
turn it about its own long axis and the SHAPE stays the same
while the STIFFNESS does not, because bending in a shell is
radial: in and out along the dome's own radius.
DOME-IN    I  5.32 in4   S  2.05 in3
a pair at one seam: both points inward, toward the centre of the dome
PANEL-IN   I  2.50 in4   S  1.63 in3
a pair at one seam: points apart, each into the middle of its own triangle
DOME-OUT   I  5.32 in4   S  2.05 in3
a pair at one seam: both points outward, away from the centre, at the sky
PANEL-OUT  I  2.50 in4   S  1.63 in3
a pair at one seam: points toward each other, across the seam
area is 6.28 in2 in all four -- rotation moves no wood
but S runs 1.63 to 2.05 in3, a factor of 1.25
Pointing the wedge at the dome's centre puts 1.25 times the bending stiffness under the same wood, for free, by turning the stick before it goes down.

chapters.title: A dome from whatever the woodlot gives
chapters.promise: I need a house, not a reference standard for symmetry.
chapters.narration: Everything so far assumed one trunk diameter. Trees do not sort themselves, and mine run ten to fifteen inches. So solve the same dome at both ends of that range. What moves is much less than you would think, and what does move lands somewhere harmless. Not one angle changes. The fold between panels is a property of the subdivision and has never heard of the log. What changes is how far each member sits back from its ideal edge, and therefore how wide the key between two panels has to be -- which is the one part that was already variable. The surface ends up slightly restless where a thin member meets a fat one. I am building somewhere to live, not something a friend can hold a straightedge against.
equations: 10-15 in logs, not one angle changes
surface steps up to 2.50 in

chapters.title: What actually moves
chapters.promise: The same shell solved at both ends of the range.
chapters.narration: The fold angles come out identical to six decimal places at both ends, which is the whole argument in one line: the geodesic solution does not know what a log is. The blank length barely shifts. The offset and the key take up the rest, and the key was already absorbing the dihedral spread, so it is doing one more job it was already shaped for. And the strength question is settled by the thinnest member on the building, not the average. At ten inches a sector still clears the crossover, so every log in the range is stiffer than the stud it replaces.
equations: the rest of this film assumes one trunk diameter. Real trees run 10 to 15 in and do not sort themselves.
solve the same dome at both ends of that range and see what moves:
fold angles: 18.029 to 22.459 deg at 10 in
fold angles: 18.029 to 22.459 deg at 15 in
IDENTICAL. not one angle in the shell depends on the log size,
because the dihedral is a property of the subdivision
what does move:
member sits back from its ideal edge, further by 0.96 in on the fat logs
key base 1.95-2.33 in thin, 2.93-3.50 in fat
blank length shifts by 0.76 in across the whole range
outer surface steps by up to 2.50 in where a thin member meets a fat one
and the strength question is settled by the THINNEST member present:
10 in sector = 9.82 in2, S 4.01 in3
= 187 % of a dressed 2x4's area and 131 % of its bending
and 10 in clears the 9.14 in crossover, so the whole range does
Mixing 10 to 15 inch logs changes no angle, moves the blank by 0.76 in, and lands the rest in the key. You get a shell with a slightly restless surface and a house that is entirely sound.

chapters.title: Why there is a key in every seam
chapters.promise: Put the variation somewhere it is cheap to be wrong.
chapters.narration: Neighbouring triangles in a geodesic shell meet at an angle, and it is not the same angle everywhere. That fold is what makes the thing a dome instead of a floor. Because each panel carries its own member, a seam is two raw sawn faces looking at each other with a gap between them, and the gap changes seam by seam. You can close it by shaving the wood to suit each neighbour, which is a different bevel every time. Or you can leave the structure alone and put the variation into a small tapered part that is not holding the building up.
equations: key base 1.56-1.87 in

chapters.title: The angle nobody wants to cut
chapters.promise: Better in a cheap part than in every stick.
chapters.narration: Here is the fold at every interior seam, and what is left over after two forty-five degree faces have folded toward each other. The spread is small in degrees and enormous in workshop terms, because it is a setup change on a saw, repeated once per seam, cut into structural members that are then not interchangeable. Moving that variation into the key means the wood stays generic and the fussy part is small, cheap and replaceable.
equations: two panels meeting along one edge are not in the same plane.
the fold between them runs 18.03 to 22.46 deg
a spread of 4.43 deg across 55 interior seams
each panel brings its own member, so a seam has two raw sawn
faces 45 deg apart before anything folds
after folding, the gap left between them runs 22.54 to 26.97 deg
which is exactly 45 deg minus the fold
there are only two ways to close a gap that is never the same:
shave the wood to suit each seam -- a different bevel, 55 times
or leave the wood alone and fit a key that varies instead
the key's base runs 1.56 to 1.87 in
one part, cut on a taper, doing what would otherwise be a setup change per seam
The key exists so the 4.43 degrees of dihedral variation live in a small replaceable part instead of in every structural member of the building.

chapters.title: One flat board, forty panels
chapters.promise: The jig is not a drawing aid. It is what makes them identical.
chapters.narration: The fixture is a flat board with the panel's triangle struck on it once, three rails, six little plates and some clamps. The rails set each member across the panel by its sawn point line, never by its bark, because the bark is the part of a log that is different every time. The red and green plates do something a drawing cannot. A sector dropped in rotated ninety degrees still looks plausible; against these plates it physically will not seat. The fixture refuses the mistake instead of relying on someone noticing it.
equations: 4 fixtures for 40 panels
rails on the sawn point, not the bark

chapters.title: The cut that is never measured
chapters.promise: One end arrives finished. The other arrives too long, on purpose.
chapters.narration: The two ends of a member are made in completely different places. The butt is cut before assembly, off the jig, to the angle its neighbour presents. It is the same cut for every member of a family, so it batches. The head is not cut at all. It arrives long, hangs off the board, and stays long while all three butts are pulled up tight and the pinwheel closes. Only then does a saw run flat along the fence and take the head off at the plane the neighbouring member has already established. Nothing is measured, and every error in stock length or butt angle walks away in the offcut instead of accumulating around the triangle.
equations: head arrives 6 in long
8.3% of raw length becomes offcut

chapters.title: What the fixture is enforcing
chapters.promise: Twelve steps, three constraints, and the offcut that buys accuracy.
chapters.narration: The fixture holds three things and nothing else: where the member sits across the panel, which way up it is turned, and the plane its head will be cut to. It is worth being precise about what the offcut buys. Every stick has some error in it. Cut both ends to a measurement and those errors add up around the triangle until the last corner does not close. Cut one end in place, against the neighbour, and the error has nowhere to accumulate. It leaves in the piece that falls on the floor.
equations: 40 triangles, 120 members, 120 corner joints -- all off one flat board
the fixture comes in 12 steps and holds three things:
a RAIL per member, set to the sawn point-axis, not the bark
a RED and a GREEN plate that make a wrongly-turned wedge physically refuse to seat
a FENCE at each head end, which is the plane the saw runs on
each member arrives with ONE cut already made:
the butt, cut to the angle its neighbour presents, batched
and one deliberate error: the head is left 6 in too long
three butts are pulled up, the loop closes, and only then is
each head sawn against its fence -- unmeasured, in place
the offcut is 60 ft per dome = 8.3 % of raw length
and 40 panels need only 4 physically different fixtures
Leaving 8.3 percent of the length as offcut is what buys the accuracy: error in stock length or butt angle leaves in the offcut instead of accumulating around the triangle.

chapters.title: What two trees make
chapters.promise: The building at the end of all of that.
chapters.narration: So this is what the arithmetic buys. Two pines off the property, converted with a chainsaw and a flat board, become a shell you can stand up in. The floor area, the height and the member count all fall out of the longest useful piece the trees give, rather than the other way round. The building is sized by the wood, not the wood by the building. That inversion is the part I would most like to hand to somebody else, because it is what makes the whole thing available to anyone with a saw and some trees.
equations: 2 trees -> 120 members
380 sq ft of floor

chapters.title: The dome the trees size
chapters.promise: Solved backwards from the longest member the wood gives.
chapters.narration: Normally you pick a dome diameter and then go and find members long enough for it. This is the same solve run the other way: start from the piece the tree actually yields and ask what shell that makes. The chord factors do not change, so the radius, the floor area and the member count all follow from one length.
equations: the tree sets the strut length, so it also sets the dome:
12 ft section, cut once = 6 ft members
the longest pinwheel member is 72.0 in
solve for the radius that makes that true:
span   22.00 ft across
height 11.00 ft at the crown
floor  380 sq ft
and the stock:
2 trees x 80 struts = 160 members
the frame needs 120
160 - 120 = 40 left for the floor and the fit-out
timber standing in the frame = 672 ft of member
Two trees, 120 members, a 22 foot dome with 380 square feet of floor -- and 40 sticks still spare.

chapters.title: The shape is doing the work
chapters.promise: None of this is a claim that split wood is better wood.
chapters.narration: A wedge from a small tree is not a stronger stick than a stud. It is a cheaper stick, a faster stick, a stick that leaves far more of the tree standing as structure instead of as shavings, and a stick that can be made without owning a factory. From a big enough tree it is also simply the stronger stick, and I gave you the diameter where that flips. But what makes it sufficient either way is the building. A triangulated shell puts its members mostly in axial load, doubles every interior edge, and asks only that the ends can be made to meet. So the honest version is not that I found a better board. It is that I picked a building that does not need one.
equations: 45 dollars an hour, in wood
120 members, 4 fixtures

chapters.title: The whole argument on one page
chapters.promise: Wood, machines, hands, rate, value, cost, strength, angle and cuts.
chapters.narration: This is everything the film just showed, in the order it showed it, with the number attached to each line. One line still carries a condition rather than a boast: below about nine inches of trunk the single wedge is the weaker member and this stops working. That stays on the page. Change the assumptions and the money moves. Change the log or the dome and the geometry moves with it, because all of it is computed and none of it is typed in.
equations: WOOD     88 % of the tree kept split, 45 % sawn -- 1.95x
MACHINE  3 fewer: SAWMILL, EDGER, PLANING MILL
HANDS    15 middle men removed between tree and wall
RATE     6 wedges/hour measured, 5 used for planning
VALUE    $10.00 of wood per wedge, $45/hour net of fuel
COST     $120 to cut this dome's frame against $1476 to buy it
STICK    226 % of a dressed stud in bending at 12 in trunk; under 9.1 in it would lose
EDGE     every interior edge carries two, 539 % of a stud's section
ANGLE    4.43 deg of dihedral variation lives in the key, not the timber
CUTS     one batched butt per member, one flush cut in place, 4 fixtures for 40 panels
Not one of those lines works on a rectangular building. They work because a triangulated shell will take any stick whose ends can be made to meet, and a split log is already that stick.

title: Two Trees, All at Once
note: Registered by the project agent repair step: the harvest lesson was in the registry without a deliverable entry.

chapters.title: Two trees
chapters.promise: The whole woodpile is standing up.
chapters.narration: It will take me 2 whole pine trees to harvest all of the wood a 300 square foot house needs. No lumber yard and no delivery truck, just the trees already standing on the property, and one small chainsaw.
bullets: {{method_a.floor_sqft}} sq ft -- the house those trees frame

chapters.title: The fell line
chapters.promise: The hinge steers the tree. The saw only sets it free.
chapters.narration: It starts with a notch, cut into the side I want it to fall toward, and then a back cut from the other side, a little higher. The strip of wood left between the two is the hinge. It steers the tree all the way over, and it is why felling gets a chapter of its own before any of this is safe to try. The saw is a 38.2 cc hardware-store model with a 16 inch bar.
bullets: {{saw.displacement_cc}} cc saw -- {{saw.bar_in}}-inch bar, off the shelf

chapters.title: All at once
chapters.promise: Every section splits at the same time.
chapters.narration: Then everything happens at once. The crown comes off, the trunk is cut into 8 sections, 6 feet each, and every section splits into 8 wedges. That is 64 struts from one tree. With 2 trees it is 128, for a frame that needs 120.

chapters.title: Why split it
chapters.promise: Split, the log keeps most of itself.
chapters.narration: Why split it instead of milling it square? Because the only wood a split loses is the width of the cut. Of the 318 board feet in this trunk, the saw takes 40 and the wedges keep 278, which is 87.4 percent of the tree standing in the frame. The honest cost is the stick itself. From a small log, a single wedge is the weaker stick in bending, and it is the triangulated shell, not the wedge, that makes it enough.
bullets: {{versus.strength_pct}}% bending strength -- {{versus.diameter_in}}-inch log: one wedge against a dressed two-by-four

chapters.title: Measured, and guessed
chapters.promise: What the next figures rest on.
chapters.narration: Before the days and the fuel, here is what those figures rest on. The fuel rate was measured, in one timed sitting with the tanks counted. The ripping hours come from the cutting rate, which was also measured. The day plan is a decision, not a result. And the size of the saw's tank is an estimate, because the listings disagree and nobody has checked this saw, so the fuel comes out as a range.
equations: MEASURED   fuel while ripping: 2 tanks an hour, one timed sitting
MEASURED   cutting rate: 30 struts in a 6-hour afternoon
DERIVED    ripping time: 120 struts at 5.0 an hour = 24 hours
DECIDED    the plan: felling days 1-2, bucking days 3-4, ripping days 5-8
ESTIMATED  the saw's tank: 0.28 to 0.37 L; the listings disagree

So the fuel is a range, and it is the ripping only

chapters.title: What it took
chapters.promise: 8 days of saw work, and a few gallons.
chapters.narration: The whole harvest takes 8 days: 2 of felling, 2 of bucking, and 4 of ripping. Ripping is the part that was timed with the fuel written down: 2 tanks an hour, for 24 hours. That is 48 tanks, and at 0.28 to 0.37 litres a tank, somewhere between 3.6 and 4.7 US gallons. Felling and bucking were never metered, so they are not in that number.

chapters.title: What the house numbers rest on
chapters.promise: Published, the author's, decided, estimated.
chapters.narration: Now the question every build gets asked: what is it worth? Before a single house figure, here is what they rest on. The published ones come from the home builders' association's cost survey, the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the builders' survey is a small one, which its own authors say. The 200,000 dollar house, the 100,000 dollar trailer, the 40 percent labor share and the 80 hours of shell work are my own round figures. The tax bracket is a decision. Everything else is an estimate, and it is labelled as one.
equations: PUBLISHED  NAHB 2024 cost survey: who gets a house's price, and 37 line items of building it (41 builders; not representative)
PUBLISHED  Census: 7.6 months, start to finish; BLS wages, May 2025
PUBLISHED  Lumber peak: $1,500 per 1,000 bd ft; +$35,872 on an average home
PUBLISHED  Manufactured homes: $86.62 a sq ft; factory split from 2002
THE AUTHOR'S  $200,000 house, $100,000 trailer, 40% labor, 80 hours of shell work
DECIDED    the 12% federal bracket; state tax left out
ESTIMATED  dealer 25%, labor by item, run share 35%, curve +25%
So every estimate below is a guess that can be changed, and says so

chapters.title: Where a house's time goes
chapters.promise: 7.6 months, most of it inside.
chapters.narration: A new house takes 7.6 months on average, from the first shovel to finished, by the Census Bureau's count, and 15.1 months when its owner builds it. One builder's week by week schedule shows where that time goes. 15 percent is the ground and the foundation. 10 percent is framing. 7.5 percent is pipes, wires and ducts. 27.5 percent is the inside: insulation, drywall, floors, trim, paint and fixtures. 10 percent is the outside, 15 percent the driveway, yard and clean up, and the last 15 percent is inspection and closing.
bullets: {{time.months}} months -- average, start to finish, Census

chapters.title: Where a house's money goes
chapters.promise: The land, the building, and the people who sell it.
chapters.narration: Now the money, in the shares the builders' survey found. Of a 200,000 dollar new house, 27,400 dollars is the land. 128,700 is the building itself. 33,400 is the builder's overhead and profit, and 10,500 is the commission, marketing and financing it takes to sell it. At the survey's national average, that much new house is only about 796 square feet.
bullets: {{house.sqft}} sq ft at the national average

chapters.title: Labor is not most of it
chapters.promise: Even at the record lumber price, labor is about a quarter.
chapters.narration: So is labor most of what you pay for? Not in a new house. Take my 40 percent of the building as labor, and it is 25.7 percent of the price. Then put the lumber at its record. In the spring of twenty twenty one, framing lumber topped 1,500 dollars a thousand board feet, and the builders worked out it added 35,872 dollars to an average new home. Price this house that way and it comes to 214,800: 82,200 in materials, 51,500 in labor, 9,800 in permits, fees and design, 27,400 for the land, 33,400 to the builder and 10,500 to sell it. Labor is 24 percent. About a quarter.
bullets: {{house.labor_pct}}% of the price is labor -- {{house.labor_share_pct}}% of the building, before the lumber peak
${{lumber.peak}} per thousand board feet -- framing lumber, the record

chapters.title: The trailer is built the other way
chapters.promise: A factory's labor is a smaller share still.
chapters.narration: A new manufactured home splits another way. Of a 100,000 dollar home, about 20,000 is the dealer's share. 46,000 is what the factory spends on materials, 16,800 is its payroll, and 17,200 is its overhead and profit. Factory labor is only 16.8 percent of the price. At the Census average of 86.62 dollars a square foot, that buys about 1,154 square feet, set up, without the land. The factory split is from the two thousand two Economic Census, the newest published in that detail, so read it as a shape more than a figure.
bullets: {{trailer.sqft}} sq ft at the Census average
{{trailer.labor_pct}}% of the price is factory labor

chapters.title: What the fortnight is worth
chapters.promise: Two weeks of one person, against buying the frame.
chapters.narration: Now the frame this film has been building. Framing is 16.6 percent of what it costs to build a new house, which is 10.7 percent of its price. For 300 square feet, bought at the national rate with the builder's share, the frame costs 9,798 dollars. The fortnight spends 497 dollars: the saw, the fuel, the hardware, and the two trees at what a timber buyer would pay for them standing. That keeps 9,301 dollars, for 80 hours of hands-on work. 116 dollars an hour. Against a manufactured home's cheaper rate it is 59. A carpenter's median wage is 29.12 an hour, and a typical worker takes home 19.69, so buying that frame would cost 498 hours of ordinary pay.
bullets: {{value.buy_hours}} hours of ordinary pay -- to buy the frame instead

chapters.title: Every part of the house
chapters.promise: The same sum, stage by stage.
chapters.narration: Here is every part of the house, done the same way for 300 square feet: what it costs to buy, what the dome way still pays in money, and how many hours of a typical worker's take-home pay the difference is worth. Fees stay fees. The foundation is shorter, because a circle has the least edge for its floor. The skin is smaller but harder to finish, and the pipes and wires run from a central column instead of around the walls. The last line is the whole floor, if every hour of the work is yours.

chapters.title: Where the saving comes from
chapters.promise: Most of it is building your own, not the shape.
chapters.narration: Stack it all up and the saving has four sources. Bought whole, the floor costs 65,100 dollars. 16,600 of that is the builder's and the seller's share, which anyone who builds their own house keeps, whatever its shape. 17,300 is labor you do yourself, paid in hours instead of money. 3,200 is lumber from your own trees instead of a yard. And 4,300 is the shape itself: 55 percent less framing, 40 percent less skin, a 12 percent shorter foundation, and runs 44 percent shorter from the central column. That leaves 23,700 dollars to pay.

chapters.title: What this does not show
chapters.promise: The half of the sum that does not flatter the dome.
chapters.narration: And what it does not show. 37 percent of what a house costs to build does not care about its shape: fees, windows, cabinets, appliances, floors, the driveway. Only the frame's hours were measured; the rest of that labor is weeks more of somebody's time, and wiring, plumbing and gas usually need a licensed trade and an inspection. A triangle is harder to finish than a flat wall, and the dome's laminate skin is its most expensive material. Against a manufactured home the gap is small: 300 square feet at a trailer's average price is 25,986 dollars, and the dome way pays 16,444 for the same parts, before your hours. And the biggest saving here, the builder's share and the labor, belongs to anyone who builds their own house, whatever its shape.
