title: The $20 Pine
note: Registered by the project agent repair step: the pine_value lesson was in the registry without a deliverable entry.

chapters.title: What is a pine worth
chapters.promise: Not one price. A ladder of them.
chapters.narration: What is a pine tree worth? Ask a timber buyer, a firewood dealer, a sawmill and a builder, and each gives a different answer, because a tree has no single value. It has a ladder of them, and the rung it reaches depends on what somebody does to it, and on how much of it they keep. Take one representative pine, the log the wedge film is built on: 60 feet of usable stem, 15 inches across at the butt and 5.5 at the top. Let us climb its ladder, one rung at a time.
bullets: {{pine.length_ft}} ft of usable stem -- {{pine.butt_in}} in at the butt, {{pine.top_in}} in at the top

chapters.title: What the ladder rests on
chapters.promise: Measured, published and mine, kept apart.
chapters.narration: Every rung rests on a figure, so here they all are before any of them is used. The tree is my representative pine, the wedge film's own log. Some figures are published: a sawmill's price for common pine, what standing pine sells for, and the size of a cord. Some are mine: a mill keeps 60 percent of the stem as the lumber it wants, splitting keeps 88, and the sawing rate and the cord price are mine too. The simulator checks both recoveries. Sawn into two by fours, this log keeps only 45 percent; split, it keeps 88.4 before any trimming. So the mill gets the benefit of the doubt, and the wedge gets no more than the model allows.
equations: THE AUTHOR'S  a representative pine: 60 ft of stem, 15 in to 5.5 in
THE AUTHOR'S  60% kept by a mill; 88% by splitting; 90 cu ft of wood a cord
THE AUTHOR'S  sawing $0.60/bd ft; a cord $275 picked up, $300 delivered
THE AUTHOR'S  $4,800 of framing for the shell; it uses 1.5 trees, 2 felled
PUBLISHED  pine $1.50/bd ft; stumpage $23.23/ton; a cord 128 cu ft stacked
CHECK  this log in the simulator: sawn to 2x4s 45%, split 88.4% before trimming
So the mill gets the benefit of the doubt, not the wedge

chapters.title: The stem, in board feet
chapters.promise: 442 board feet, and about $24 standing.
chapters.narration: The usable stem is a long, tapering cone: 36.8 cubic feet of solid wood. A cubic foot holds 12 board feet, so that is 442 board feet, the most that any method could ever get out of it. Green, it weighs about 1.01 tons, and at the published stumpage of $23.23 a ton, it sells standing for about 24 dollars. That is the twenty-dollar pine. Every rung above this one is something somebody does to it.

chapters.title: Burned, it is heat
chapters.promise: Burned, it is worth its heat: $113.
chapters.narration: The first rung up is fire. This stem is 36.8 cubic feet of solid wood. A cord is 4 feet high, 4 deep and 8 long, 128 cubic feet stacked, but air fills the gaps, and only about 90 of those cubic feet are wood. So the stem makes 0.41 of a cord. At 275 dollars a cord picked up, that is 113 dollars, or about 123 delivered. That values the tree for its heat. Every rung above this one values it for its shape.
bullets: {{pine.cord_solid_ft3}} cu ft of wood in a cord

chapters.title: Split, not sawn
chapters.promise: A mill wants rectangles. A wedge takes the log as it is.
chapters.narration: Now shape. A sawmill has to turn a round log into rectangles, and everything outside them leaves as slabs, edgings and sawdust. The picture is the simulator's, packing this log with two by fours, and it keeps only 45 percent. A good mill cutting mixed sizes does better, so I give it 60 percent. Splitting follows the round log instead of fighting it. From the same stem it keeps 88 percent, 389 board feet, where the mill keeps 265. That is 124 more board feet of usable wood from one tree, because the corners of a log are not bad wood. They are only not rectangular.
bullets: {{pine.extra_bf}} bd ft more, from one tree

chapters.title: Almost half as much again
chapters.promise: 46.7% more wood, 70% less thrown away.
chapters.narration: Put the two recoveries side by side. 88 percent over 60 is 1.467, so splitting gets 46.7 percent more usable wood out of the same tree. Now look at what is left behind. The mill leaves 40 percent of the stem, 177 board feet of it. Splitting leaves 12 percent, 53. That is 70 percent less of the tree thrown away, from the same tree, with the same saw.

chapters.title: The same wood from fewer trees
chapters.promise: 2 trees split give as much wood as 2.93 sawn.
chapters.narration: A 300 square foot shell needs 2 of these trees felled. Each one, split, gives 389 board feet, so the pair gives 778. A mill keeping 60 percent gets 265 from a tree, so to match the pair it would need 2.93 trees. Put the other way round, the mill's way needs almost half as many trees again, and a tree not cut is a tree still standing, or a tree left for the next building.

chapters.title: Priced as lumber
chapters.promise: Priced as wood, splitting is worth $186 more a tree.
chapters.narration: Now put a price on the wood. The split yield, 389 board feet, at one sawmill's list price for common pine of $1.50 a board foot, is worth 584 dollars. The sawn yield, 265 board feet, is worth 398. That is 186 dollars more from one tree, and 372 from the shell's 2. And the sawn path still has to pay for the sawing: at my rate of $0.60 a board foot, about 159 dollars for this tree.

chapters.title: Built, it replaces framing
chapters.promise: Not what the wood would sell for. What it does.
chapters.narration: The next rung is not a price for wood at all. In the dome, these trees become a shell of 300 square feet. At 100 dollars a square foot, with framing 16 percent of it, the framing that shell replaces is worth 4,800 dollars, the figure the last film built. The frame uses 90 feet of trunk, 1.5 trees' worth, but 2 are felled, so I divide by 2: each tree's share is 2,400 dollars. That is use value: not what the wood would fetch, but what you no longer have to buy, because the wood is doing the job.

chapters.title: Carried on a mortgage
chapters.promise: What the same framing costs when it is borrowed.
chapters.narration: Most framing is not paid for in cash. It rides on a mortgage. On a 30 year loan at 6.5 percent, 4,800 dollars of framing becomes 10,922 dollars of payments, and this tree's half of that is 5,461. Read this rung carefully. It is nominal dollars, paid a month at a time for 30 years, not money in your hand today. But it is money a household never has to send to a lender, because a tree did the job instead.

chapters.title: The ladder
chapters.promise: One tree, every rung.
chapters.narration: Now put the rungs together. Standing, about 24 dollars. Burned, 113. Sawn into lumber, 398. Split into wedge stock, 584. Built into structure, 2,400. And as the mortgage payments that structure avoids, 5,461, nominal, over 30 years. It is the same tree on every rung. What changes is how much of it is kept, and how far along the chain it travels before anyone has to pay for the next step.

chapters.title: The wood did not get better
chapters.promise: It got used.
chapters.narration: Compare the structure rung with the ones below it. 2,400 dollars is 21 times what the tree brings as firewood, 6 times its sawn lumber, and 4.1 times its split stock. The wood did not get better between those rungs. The same fibres, from the same tree, stopped being sold as a commodity and started doing a job. The biggest step on this ladder is not from the woods to the mill. It is from material to function.

chapters.title: What the tree is worth to me
chapters.promise: What it replaces, less what it costs me to make it do so.
chapters.narration: So here is the valuation that matters to a builder. A tree is worth to me what it can replace, less the cash it costs to process, less what my own hours could have earned instead. This tree replaces 2,400 dollars of framing. Its share of the work is 40 hours, and at 25 dollars an hour take-home, that is 1,000 dollars of my time. Its share of the cash is half the shell's 800, 400 dollars. That leaves 1,000 dollars. A pine that sells for 24 dollars standing is worth 1,000 to the person who builds with it, after paying for their own time. With the fortnight's actual receipts of 497 dollars, it is 1,152.

chapters.title: The household as the whole chain
chapters.promise: Logger, mill, yard, framer and lender, kept at home.
chapters.narration: This is vertical integration, at the scale of one household. A commercial house pays every hand between the stump and the wall: the logger, the hauler, the mill, the kiln, the yard, the framer, and very often the lender. Each one takes a margin, and every margin is inside the price. This method does not make those businesses unnecessary for everyone. It lets one owner do the few steps a chainsaw and a jig can do, and keep what those steps would have cost. That is where the rungs above the wood come from.

chapters.title: What the ladder does not say
chapters.promise: The generous figures, and the ones against me.
chapters.narration: Three cautions, because a ladder like this is easy to oversell. First, my mill figure is generous to the mill: the simulator's own packing of this log keeps 45 percent, and I used 60. Second, my sawing rate may be high. A survey of portable sawmill owners in 2010 found them charging $0.20 to $0.30 a board foot. Prices have risen since, but the sawn path may cost less than I said. Third, the top two rungs are not cash. The 2,400 dollars counts only if you would otherwise have bought the frame, and the financed rung is nominal payments, spread over 30 years.

chapters.title: Thousands of dollars of structure
chapters.promise: The difference is what you do with it.
chapters.narration: So a twenty-dollar pine is not a twenty-dollar pine. On the stump it brings about 24 dollars. Burned, 113. Sawn, 398. Split, 584. Built into a shell, it replaces 2,400 dollars of framing, and 5,461 of payments on a loan. The tree is the same on every rung. What moves it up the ladder is how much of it you keep, and how many of the steps between the tree and the wall you are willing to take yourself.

title: Why Build This Way
note: Registered by the project agent repair step: the why_build lesson was in the registry without a deliverable entry.

chapters.title: How much shelter does an hour buy
chapters.promise: Not how cheap the house is. How much shelter an hour buys.
chapters.narration: The case for this dome is not that it makes a house cheap. It is that it changes the trade between a person, their time, raw wood and shelter. This is one shell, 300 square feet, from 2 trees. The question worth asking is not how cheap the house is, but how much shelter one hour of your life can buy, and this way of building changes the answer.

chapters.title: A long chain, and a short one
chapters.promise: Income, tax, store, contractor, loan. Or tree, wedge, jig, shell.
chapters.narration: Conventional housing asks you to join a long chain. You sell hours for money, pay tax on it, buy lumber that was sawn, dried, shipped, stocked and marked up, hire the labor to put it together, and very often borrow for all of it for decades. This system shortens the chain. A tree is split into wedges, the wedges go into a jig, and the jig makes the shell. Part of your labor turns straight into structure, without passing through a paycheck, a tax bill, a store and a loan on the way.

chapters.title: The tree is the product
chapters.promise: Split, not sawn: the round log keeps its wood.
chapters.narration: A sawmill forces a round tree into rectangles. The wedge does not. An 8 inch log splits into 8 sectors, and each one keeps 6.28 square inches of wood, against 5.25 in a dressed two by four. That does not make every wedge stronger than every board; from a log that small, a single wedge is the weaker stick in bending. What it means is that very little happens between the tree and the frame: 8 operations, where a graded board takes 14.
bullets: {{versus.wedge_area_in2}} sq in, one wedge -- from an {{versus.diameter_in}}-inch log
{{route.wedge_steps}} operations, tree to frame -- a graded board takes {{route.mill_steps}}

chapters.title: The geometry does some of the work
chapters.promise: A wedge arrives with its angle already in it.
chapters.narration: An eighth of a log arrives with two split faces 45 degrees apart. The dome's panels fold at only 2 angles, 18.03 and 22.46 degrees. The wedge does not match them exactly, but it starts with useful angle already in it, and a shaped key takes up the rest, so nobody has to manufacture every angle out of a rectangle. That is the rule the whole system runs on: do not make every piece perfect; make the system force imperfect pieces into the right relationship.

chapters.title: Locate first, cut second
chapters.promise: The jig solves the geometry once, not for every stick.
chapters.narration: Custom timber work means measuring, transferring angles, fitting, checking and trimming, again and again. Here the jig decides where each member belongs and which way it turns. The members are left long, their ends hang past the triangle, and once the jig holds all three in their true relationship, the excess is cut flush. Locate accurately first; cut accurately second. The hard geometry is solved once, in the jig, and a complicated dome becomes 40 repeats of one job.

chapters.title: The figures this rests on
chapters.promise: The author's round numbers, beside the published ones.
chapters.narration: Now the money, and first what it rests on. These are my own round figures: bought space at 100 dollars a square foot, framing as 16 percent of it, 80 hours of hands-on shell work, and a 6.5 percent mortgage over 30 years. Beside them are the published ones. A new manufactured home averages 86.62 dollars a square foot, and a new site-built house about 217 without the land. My figures sit on the cautious side of both.
equations: THE AUTHOR'S  $100 a sq ft; framing 16% of it; 80 hours of shell work
THE AUTHOR'S  6.5% for 30 years; $25 an hour take-home; $800 cash
PUBLISHED  new manufactured home: $86.62 a sq ft (Census)
PUBLISHED  new site-built house: $216.94 a sq ft without land (NAHB)
PUBLISHED  framing 16.6% of building cost; median take-home $19.69 an hour (BLS)
So the author's figures sit on the cautious side of the published ones

chapters.title: What an hour produces
chapters.promise: Not a paycheck. Value you no longer have to buy.
chapters.narration: 300 square feet in 80 hours is 3.75 square feet an hour. At 100 dollars a square foot, that floor is worth 30,000 dollars finished, but framing did not create all of it; plumbing, wiring, windows and finishes are still to come. So take only the framing, 16 percent of it: 4,800 dollars. Divided by 80 hours, that is 60 dollars an hour. Nobody hands me that as a wage. A wage is what someone pays you for your hour; this is what your hour saves you from having to buy.

chapters.title: Why the hour beats a wage
chapters.promise: It replaces the wood as well as the work.
chapters.narration: Of that 4,800 dollars, the labor is 40 percent: 1,920 dollars, and over the same 80 hours that is 24 dollars an hour. That is the framing labor alone. The dome way produces 60, which is 2.5 times as much, an index of 250 where framing labor alone scores a hundred. Be clear about where that comes from: it is one over the labor share. You supply the labor, and you also replace the wood you would have bought. That second part is exactly what a wage comparison leaves out.
bullets: {{why.index}} value index -- framing labor alone scores a hundred

chapters.title: Debt makes it larger
chapters.promise: An avoided dollar can be an avoided interest-bearing dollar.
chapters.narration: Now suppose that framing would otherwise ride on a 30 year mortgage at 6.5 percent. Then 4,800 dollars does not stay 4,800; it becomes 10,922 dollars of payments. Spread over the same 80 hours, that is 137 dollars an hour. That is not a wage, and it is not today's money: it is payments that never have to be made, stretched across 30 years. Today's value is still 60 dollars an hour. But a dollar avoided before it enters a mortgage is a dollar that never collects interest.

chapters.title: Interest builds nothing
chapters.promise: No bedroom, no wall, no square foot.
chapters.narration: Take a 100,000 dollar mortgage at the same rate. Over 30 years you pay 127,544 dollars of interest on it, 227,544 in all. At 100 dollars a square foot, the interest alone would buy 1,275 square feet. Interest builds no bedroom, no workshop, no wall. It is the price of having the house before you have the money. Building directly does something else: effort becomes equity. Hours become members, members become panels, and panels become square feet.
bullets: {{why.interest_sqft}} sq ft the interest would buy

chapters.title: Count it in hours of your life
chapters.promise: Money is stored labor.
chapters.narration: Here is the comparison that matters most. Buying that 4,800 dollar frame, at 25 dollars an hour take-home, takes 192 hours of work. Building it takes 80 hours, plus 32 more to earn its 800 dollars of cash, 112 hours in all. That keeps 80 hours of your life, 2 full working weeks, on one shell. And the typical worker takes home less than 25, about 19.69 an hour, which makes buying cost 244 hours instead.
bullets: {{why.take_home_buy_hours}} hours, median pay -- to buy it at ${{wage.take_home}} an hour take-home

chapters.title: When to build, and when to buy
chapters.promise: Build while your hour creates more than it earns.
chapters.narration: This is a rule, not an ideology. What building earns per hour is the money it avoids, less the cash it still costs, over the hours it takes. 4,800 less 800 is 4,000, and over 80 hours that is 50 dollars an hour. If you take home less than that, those hours are worth more building than working extra to buy the same frame. If you take home a good deal more, buying may be the better use of your time. Build while the value your hour creates beats what it earns after tax.

chapters.title: Out of the commodity chain
chapters.promise: Every member from a nearby tree is one less price shock.
chapters.narration: A conventional house also runs a long critical path, about 33 weeks from start to finish, carrying financing, weather, scheduling and overhead the whole way. And it rides on commodity lumber. In the spring of twenty twenty one, framing lumber topped 1,500 dollars a thousand board feet and added 35,872 dollars to an average new home. A dome still needs fasteners, glazing, wiring, plumbing and a foundation. But every structural member cut from a nearby tree instead of bought at a yard is one less exposure to that market. A tree on the land stops being scenery and becomes inventory.
bullets: {{why.weeks}} weeks, a new house -- start to finish, the Census average
${{lumber.added}} added by the lumber spike -- lumber topped ${{lumber.peak}} per thousand board feet

chapters.title: The economic score
chapters.promise: One shell, on one sheet.
chapters.narration: Put one cycle on a single sheet. 300 square feet of shell in 80 hours. 4,800 dollars of commercial framing displaced. 60 dollars an hour of production value, 2.5 times the framing labor alone. 10,922 dollars of mortgage payments avoided, 137 an hour, and not a wage. 80 hours of life kept. A break-even of 50 dollars an hour. And one shell a year for 30 years is 144,000 dollars of framing and 9,000 square feet.

chapters.title: What the model does not promise
chapters.promise: A model, not a guarantee.
chapters.narration: None of this is a guarantee; it is a model. The 60 dollars an hour is money not spent, not money earned, and it only counts if you would otherwise have bought the frame. The frame is 16.6 percent of what a new house costs to build, and permits, wiring, plumbing, windows and finishes are still ahead, some of it needing a licensed trade and an inspection. The house labor budget I once compared against was 80,000 dollars; the builders' survey puts that house's labor nearer 51,491, about 39.01 dollars per working hour of the build, so the dome's 60 is 154 percent of it, not the same. And my 4,800 dollar frame is cheaper than either published price, 5,186 at a manufactured home's rate and 9,798 at a new house's, so the case is made at its weakest.
bullets: {{why.burn_pct}}% of the survey's rate -- ${{why.burn}} a work-hour, not ${{why.author_burn}}

chapters.title: The why
chapters.promise: More shelter from each hour of a finite life.
chapters.narration: So the reason to build this way is not that domes look different, or that ordinary houses are bad, or that lumber is useless. It is that conventional housing is built around buying highly processed materials and buying specialized labor, and this asks whether the owner can take back part of both. If the answer is yes, the rest follows: less processing, less bought lumber and labor, less financing, less interest, less exposure to prices and schedules, and more use of what is already standing on the land. The question is not how cheap the house is, but how much shelter an hour of your life can buy. On these numbers, this way of building changes that exchange rate. That is the reason.
bullets: {{why.kept_hours}} hours of life kept, one shell

title: All Domes
note: The Dome Creator's whole catalogue drawn by the Creator's own renderer -- grain, glass, mirrors, foundations and the fit-out inside -- one dome built step by step in the tool's own construction order, then every menu swept one setting at a time, eight random draws, and the permutation count.
fit: Every dome type in turn. Use the pad as the turntable: hide the wedge dome while another stands there, bring it back for the wedge chapters.

chapters.title: All domes
chapters.promise: Every building the Dome Creator makes, drawn by the Dome Creator.
chapters.narration: The Dome Creator is a walkable customizer with twelve finished designs in it, and this is all of them -- but not the way a film has shown them before. Until now the films rebuilt a preset's geometry and then re-drew it with their own tubes and triangles, which is a sketch of the building. These are the tool's own meshes, running through the tool's own shader. The wood has grain, the glass has a highlight, the mirror tiles are reflecting a tree line, and each of these is assembling itself in the order its construction record says to build it.

chapters.title: The catalogue, counted
chapters.promise: Twelve buildings, fit-out included, none of it typed in.
chapters.narration: Start with all twelve on one screen, because the spread is the point. The same engine makes a six hundred square foot treehouse dome and a three thousand square foot lodge, and the only things that changed are a frequency, a radius and a material list. The equipment count on the right is the part the old catalogue film could not show at all.

chapters.title: What is declared, and what is measured
chapters.promise: Prices are declared inputs. Everything else is read off the model.
chapters.narration: Before any dollar figure, here is where the dollars come from. The densities and unit prices live in one file in this project, they are declared inputs, and they are the only numbers in this film that were typed by a person. Every quantity they get multiplied by -- areas, lengths, counts, weights -- is measured off the model that drew the building you are looking at. Change a price in that file and the next render says the new number without anybody editing a script.

chapters.title: Timber Workshop
chapters.promise: The one the tool opens on, and the one every sweep starts from.
chapters.narration: Dimensional lumber on metal brackets, plywood between the struts, a concrete slab under all of it, and a working shop on the floor: benches, a machine station, a tool chest, shelving, an office corner. Watch what happens when the roof comes off. That equipment is not set dressing. Every piece has a weight, a price and a power draw in the model, and the wiring on the floor was routed to reach it.

chapters.title: Glass Studio Loft
chapters.promise: Four frequency, glazed, on a deck: the expensive, beautiful end.
chapters.narration: Raise the frequency and the shell gets rounder and much more complicated: two hundred and fifty struts instead of a hundred and sixty five. Every panel here is glass, which is why you can see the furniture through the wall, and why the shader is putting a highlight on the panels facing the sun. It stands on a wood deck rather than a slab.

chapters.title: Split-Log Homestead
chapters.promise: Hubless, framed from split logs, cedar shakes over the top.
chapters.narration: This is the design this whole project argues for. Two frequency, hubless doubled framing, quarter wedges split straight from logs. There is not one hub connector in the building. Every triangle brings its own three members and bolts to its neighbours, and the cedar shakes you can see are a cladding layer sitting over the sheathing, not a texture painted on it.

chapters.title: Whole Trunk Lodge - 20 ft
chapters.promise: Whole trunks, sized so the longest member is just under twenty feet.
chapters.narration: Now use the tree whole. The radius is set so the longest member lands just under twenty feet, which is what two people can actually move. Sixty five round trunks, canvas stretched between them, gravel underneath. It is the largest floor in the catalogue by a wide margin and it is framed from the fewest pieces of anything here.

chapters.title: Grow Dome
chapters.promise: Aluminium and polycarbonate: the greenhouse configuration.
chapters.narration: The same three frequency skeleton as the workshop, framed in aluminium and glazed in twinwall polycarbonate, with grow racks and water storage inside. The geometry did not change at all. Only the material list did, and the price came down by nearly half.

chapters.title: Hex Cell Pavilion
chapters.promise: A hexagonal cell frame in structural steel.
chapters.narration: Not everything here is triangulated the same way. The hex cell style groups the geometry into hexagonal tiles on a steel frame, and the panels are composite hexagons with a seam bead around each one. It is heavier and dearer than anything timber, and it looks like nothing else on the site.

chapters.title: Continuous Steel Arc Hangar
chapters.promise: Curved ribs running over the shell instead of straight struts.
chapters.narration: The hangar swaps short straight struts for twelve continuous steel arcs and three rings, with fabrication and site power equipment inside it. Two frequency, eight metre radius, open between the ribs. This is what the same geometry looks like when a steel shop builds it instead of a carpenter.

chapters.title: Rebar Garden Dome
chapters.promise: A dense meridian and ring lattice, bent from rebar.
chapters.narration: Rebar is the cheapest structural steel there is, and it bends, so the tool draws it as twenty two meridians and seven rings rather than sticks between hubs. Seven thousand dollars, which is the cheapest building in the catalogue, and it is the one closest to what people actually put up in a back yard on a weekend.

chapters.title: Concrete Monocoque Form
chapters.promise: The frame as formwork for a poured shell.
chapters.narration: Here the frame is not the building, it is the formwork. Rebar and shuttering panels carry a poured concrete shell, with shoring jacks, scaffold, a mixer and a bender on the floor. The dome is doing the thing concrete is best at, standing in pure compression, and it is by some distance the heaviest thing here.

chapters.title: Woodland Hex Mirror
chapters.promise: Hexagonal mirror tiles that reflect the site back at you.
chapters.narration: The mirror designs exist because the renderer can do it. Those tiles are reflecting a sky and a tree line the shader computes per pixel, which is why the dome looks different from every angle as the camera moves. Structurally it is the same three frequency shell as the workshop.

chapters.title: Woodland Square Mirror
chapters.promise: The same trick at four frequency, on square tiles.
chapters.narration: Four frequency on a steel frame, square mirror tiles instead of hexagons. More panels, each smaller, so the reflection breaks up finer. Between the two mirror designs you can see exactly what frequency does to a faceted surface: it stops looking like a machine and starts looking like a curve.

chapters.title: Treehouse Canopy Dome
chapters.promise: An elevated dome on a supported timber platform.
chapters.narration: The smallest one, and the only one that is not on the ground. A two frequency hex tile dome on a timber platform with a central trunk, six posts, braces and a ladder, all of which the tool builds because the foundation menu has a treehouse platform in it. Six hundred square feet, up in the canopy.

chapters.title: One dome, step by step
chapters.promise: The tool's own construction order, played end to end.
chapters.narration: The mesh is not assembled in a random order. The builder emits it the way a trailer home is manufactured: site prep, then the slab, then the floor layout, the frame from the base ring upward, the hubs, the doorway, the sheathing bottom to top, the cladding, then rough electrical, rough plumbing, partitions, equipment, and finally the monitoring system. The ring on the floor is where the record says the crew is standing for the step on screen, and the hours are the tool's own estimate for the work done so far.

chapters.title: The labour model, phase by phase
chapters.promise: Three hundred and forty eight work steps, grouped.
chapters.narration: Those steps add up, and grouping them says something useful about where a dome's time actually goes. The frame, which is the part everybody pictures when they think about building a dome, is not the expensive phase in hours. This is a model, not a stopwatch, and I want to be clear about that: it is an estimate attached to each work step. But it is the same estimate applied to every design, so comparing two of them is fair even where the absolute number is soft.
equations: Timber Workshop: 348 work steps, in build order:
Site               2 steps    14.0 h
Frame            165 steps    19.8 h
Joins             61 steps    12.2 h
Openings           1 steps     2.0 h
Sheathing        105 steps    42.0 h
Fit-out           13 steps     5.1 h
Commissioning      1 steps     2.0 h
total 97.1 hours of work
two people, eight hour days: 6.1 days
97 hours is the tool's estimate, not a stopwatch -- but it is the same estimate for every design, so the comparisons between them hold even where the absolute number does not

chapters.title: Frequency
chapters.promise: One radius, four subdivisions, all four built.
chapters.narration: Now the menus, one at a time, and this is the first of them. Same radius, same material, same foundation: only the number of times each face is divided changes. One frequency is twenty five struts in one length. Four frequency is two hundred and fifty in six lengths. Frequency buys you a smoother shell and charges you in part variety, which is the thing that actually slows a build down.

chapters.title: The four dials, and why they are countable
chapters.promise: Radius, strut width, recess and pad size move in fixed steps.
chapters.narration: The tool also has sliders, and sliders look like they have infinite settings. They do not: each one moves in a fixed step, and those steps are written in the menu code, so they can be counted exactly like the drop-downs can. And not one of them changes the part count. Doubling the radius gives you four times the floor off the same list of operations, which is the whole economic argument for this shape.
equations: the sliders are not continuous -- the tool moves them in steps:
Radius                 2 to 15  step 0.5     27 settings   m
Strut width       0.02 to 0.35  step 0.005   67 settings   m
Recess depth      0.05 to 0.95  step 0.05    19 settings   fraction of strut depth
Foundation size       1 to 1.6  step 0.05    13 settings   x radius
446,823 settings from four dials, and not one of them changes the part count: frequency alone decides how many pieces there are

chapters.title: Six ways to join the same sticks
chapters.promise: Hub and strut, hubless, hex cell, arcs, lattice, formwork.
chapters.narration: The frame style menu changes how the members meet, and it changes the building far more than the material does. Hub and strut is the classic. Hubless doubled gives every triangle its own three members. Hex cell groups them into hexagons. The arc and lattice styles throw out straight struts entirely and run continuous ribs over the shell. Formwork treats the frame as shuttering for something poured.

chapters.title: The six, counted -- including where the tool argues with itself
chapters.promise: And one disagreement inside the tool, said out loud.
chapters.narration: Here they are as numbers, off the same shell. The interesting one is at the bottom, and it is not flattering. Two of these styles report hub connectors in the bill of materials that their own assembly never fits. The picture and the price disagree. The picture is the one to believe, because it is the assembly, so treat those two totals as high by their hub line. I would rather this film state that than quietly average it away.

chapters.title: Eight cross sections
chapters.promise: Round tube to quarter wedge, all at the same width.
chapters.narration: The strut shape menu decides what every member is cut from. Round tube, solid rod, rebar, whole trunk, square tube, dimensional lumber, hex strut, and the quarter wedge this project is built around. All eight are drawn at the same nominal width, so what you are seeing is the profile the tool sweeps along each member, and the amount of material each one actually contains. The ninth is the same quarter wedge with its bark turned outward, because that is a menu of its own and it only means anything here.

chapters.title: Eight materials
chapters.promise: The same frame, priced and weighed eight ways.
chapters.narration: The material menu carries a density and a price per kilogram, so changing it changes what the frame weighs and what it costs without touching a single dimension. Structural steel and timber frame the identical building. One of them is fifteen times the weight of the other.

chapters.title: Sixteen finishes
chapters.promise: Eight frame colours in front, eight panel tints behind.
chapters.narration: Two menus that change everything about how a building looks and nothing at all about what it costs: the frame colour and the panel tint. Front row is the frame, back row is the skin. It is worth knowing which of these decisions are free, because they are the ones you can change your mind about on the day.

chapters.title: Sixteen panel types
chapters.promise: Everything the tool can put between the struts.
chapters.narration: This is the menu that decides both what a dome looks like and what it costs. Open, plywood, glass, acrylic, twinwall, sheeting, insulated panel, shingle, metal, solar, canvas, hex composite, hex mirror, square mirror, concrete form, precast. Every one of these is the same shell underneath. Watch the mirrors on the bottom row and the solar cells above them: those are patterns the shader computes, not pictures pasted on.

chapters.title: Which menu is the expensive one
chapters.promise: One design, one menu at a time, every setting priced.
chapters.narration: So which of these choices actually costs money? Hold everything else at the workshop and price every setting of each menu in turn. The answer is that the covering and the frame material swing the price by tens of thousands, the geometry barely moves it, and three of the menus are free. That is good news, because the covering is the decision you can defer, stage, or upgrade later. The frame is the one you have to get right on day one.

change one menu at a time, price every setting:

and 3 menus cost nothing at all: frame colour, panel colour, wedge curve
frame material swings the price by $74,622 on the same geometry -- the shape is not what you are paying for

chapters.title: Nine cladding layers
chapters.promise: What goes over the sheathing, in three stackable slots.
chapters.narration: Over the panels the tool will stack up to three cladding layers: plastic film, house wrap, foam, asphalt shingles, cedar shakes, an EPDM membrane, a green roof, or a poured concrete shell. Each one has a thickness, so they sit visibly outside the shell, and each covers only the panels that are neither open nor windows -- which is the model being careful for you.

chapters.title: Seven foundations
chapters.promise: Bare ground to a treehouse platform.
chapters.narration: Underneath, seven choices, and the tool builds each one properly: grass, gravel, a slab, a wood deck, stone pavers, bare ground, and a treehouse platform that comes with a trunk, six posts, braces and a ladder. The pad is sized from the dome's own radius, and it is priced by the square metre, which is why the platform is the dearest thing in this row by a long way.

chapters.title: Four ways to divide a floor
chapters.promise: Nothing, markings, low walls, full walls.
chapters.narration: Inside, the floor is split into ten sections -- a centre hub and nine wedges -- and each one can be assigned a room type from a list of sixteen. The partition menu decides whether those sections are just painted on the slab or actually framed. Roofs off for this one, because there is no other way to see it.

chapters.title: The part nobody films
chapters.promise: Equipment, framed walls, plumbing -- and the circuits nobody has.
chapters.narration: Here is the whole reason to draw the tool's real mesh rather than a shell. The homestead has twelve pieces of equipment on the floor, each with a price, a weight and a power draw. It has seven partition walls framed to a real height. It has hot, cold and drain lines run from a utility stub to every fixture in it. What it does not have is a single circuit, and neither does any other design in the catalogue. Conduit runs have to start at a battery bank or a charge controller, and not one preset ships with either. Put a battery bank on the floor and the wiring appears on its own.

chapters.title: What the fit-out costs
chapters.promise: The dome is the cheap part of the dome.
chapters.narration: Add the equipment, the walls and the plumbing up, and they are a serious fraction of what this building costs -- on a design whose shell is split logs and plywood. The electrical line is the one to read carefully. Zero is what the catalogue reports, and that is a fact about the presets rather than about domes: add the power source and the model routes twenty two metres of conduit without being asked twice. The shape saves you on envelope. It does not save you on anything that plugs in.

conduit runs start at a battery bank or a charge controller,

chapters.title: Eight the dice picked
chapters.promise: Random settings, built and priced, seed on screen.
chapters.narration: Every dome so far was chosen. These eight were not: the film drew them at random from the menus, built whatever came out, and priced it. The seed is on screen, so anyone can run the same draw and get the same eight buildings. Some of them are sensible. At least one of them is a thing nobody would ever build, which is the honest shape of a combination space this large.

chapters.title: How many domes that is
chapters.promise: Sixteen billion shells, and the film that would take.
chapters.narration: So how many buildings can this tool actually make? Multiply the menus. Then take the honest deduction, because some settings do nothing in some combinations, and count only the shells that genuinely differ. The number is still sixteen and a half billion. At three seconds each, showing every one of them would take fifteen centuries of film, so this one does the only sane thing instead: every setting of every menu, at least once, which is what you have just watched.

chapters.title: Open the tool and check any of it
chapters.promise: Load the preset. Read the bill of materials.
chapters.narration: That is the catalogue, every menu in the customizer, and the count of what they add up to. Nothing here was asserted: every figure was read off a model this film rebuilt while it was rendering, and every building was drawn by the tool's own renderer rather than an impression of it. So do not take my word for any of it. Open the Dome Creator, press the preset button until you reach the one you want, and read the bill of materials. It will say what this film said.

classes = 4

chapters.title: The classes
chapters.promise: A local Tuscaloosa-area firewood seller currently lists $275/cord pickup and $300/cord delivered.
chapters.narration: Alabama Extension defines a cord as 128 cubic feet of stacked wood, about 90 cubic feet of solid wood, and a 15-inch pine is about 0.35-0.45 cord. Radial processing gives 1 log to 2 to 4 to 8 sectors; 8 times 60 feet of usable stem is 480 linear feet, cut into six-foot members that is 80 structural blanks per tree.

title: Bring Your Own Dome
note: The annotated-transcript revision: animated iris, central services, movable partitions, wedge channels, staged growth, and a starter-first budget. Includes the shared contact outro.

chapters.title: A home you keep
chapters.promise: BRING YOUR OWN DOME
chapters.narration: Bring your own dome. Build a home. Improve it. Take it with you.

chapters.title: An RV park, for houses
chapters.promise: Serviced pads. You bring the home.
chapters.narration: Think: fancier trailer park. Or maybe better, a stationary RV park where the thing you park is a house you built and can take apart again. A landowner builds a circular service pad. A dome owner arrives with their home, sets it down on the pad, and plugs in. These domes come from the Dome Creator and the wedge simulator. The same tools that design them draw them here.

chapters.title: Why would someone host a dome?
chapters.promise: Income from the pad. Fewer household repairs.
chapters.narration: Why would people want to host these things? Cash money. Income from land, without also buying and maintaining the home somebody else lives in. We know the pains of landlords. We know the pains of tenants. I want to bridge the two so the arrangement works for both. They love me, they love each other. That is the dream, anyway. The host still looks after the pad and the services. But replacing somebody's kitchen, sofa, or bedroom carpet is no longer the host's business.

chapters.title: Why buy the dome?
chapters.promise: Start small. Upgrade the home you own.
chapters.narration: And why put your own money into a dome? Because a small personal home can start simple, then become more comfortable, larger, and better equipped as your life changes. My target for the basic trailer model of this system is a five thousand dollar dome, relying on the pad for the essentials. That is a design target, not a finished-home quote. Put the durable money into hardware planned for the current dome and two sizes beyond it. Then collect the longer members for the next build over time. We will come back to exactly what that means.

chapters.title: Two people. Clear responsibilities.
chapters.promise: Amber: the pad host. Cyan: the dome owner.
chapters.narration: Amber is the pad host: the deck, the service connections, the meter. Cyan is the dome owner: the house and everything they do to it. The important line stays in the same place. The host provides the site. The resident owns the home. You still pay for the ground and the services, but the house you improve is yours. Both sides keep control of their own part, with fewer things held in common and a clearer goodbye when it is time to move.

chapters.title: The reserved spot
chapters.promise: Utilities in the center. Choices around them.
chapters.narration: The middle of the pad is the spot every builder knows to reserve for utilities. It is not the only way to do it. It is the way I want this system to work. Power, water, and drain come up inside the footprint. The connections do not need to cross the doorway. From the center, supply lines and wiring can go upward, outward, and into accessible routes around the shell. Drainage stays down at the floor. You can change the rooms around that known service location instead of redesigning the whole house every time your life changes.

chapters.title: Your life changes. The rooms can too.
chapters.promise: Bedroom + office. Later, a larger bedroom.
chapters.narration: Split a big bedroom to make an office. Three years later you retire, stop needing the office, and open the bedroom back up. I live in a trailer. Four bedrooms, living room, den, office, two bathrooms, kitchen, dining area. We have all the allotments of a domicile. But the way we need that space has changed. I was gone for six years. I came back. Three people becomes four, and eventually that same house could be too much for one person. A dome with movable, nonstructural partitions gives us a way to reallocate the space. The shell stays. The room plan can change.

chapters.title: One pad. More than one dome size.
chapters.promise: An iris, with leaves you can actually see move.
chapters.narration: So what is a pad? Start with the ground, then a deck or prepared surface, and an acceptor rim that the dome latches to. The basic rim can be fixed. This upgrade is an iris: leaves moving on a track, opening and closing like a camera aperture. Watch the contact points move inward, then outward. The concept spans roughly twenty to forty feet. The deck stays in place while the acceptor changes size. A host could accommodate several dome sizes with one adjustable assembly. That mechanism is a development concept, and it belongs in the upgrade column.

chapters.title: The deluxe version
chapters.promise: Turn toward the sun. Or choose a different view.
chapters.narration: Then there is the top-line version: a rotating foundation. This is the expensive one. And honestly, it is just freaking cool. Maybe today I want the window facing the street. Maybe I have someone over and want it facing the private, fenced corner instead. Maybe I want the morning sun on my face. Maybe tomorrow I definitely do not. You could change the way the house faces even without a single solar panel. With an asymmetric solar layout, turning also gives you a way to aim that part of the shell. The bearing, drive, and rotating utility connections need their own development. This is future deluxe hardware.

chapters.title: The wedge dome's service channels
chapters.promise: Up the center. Along the shell. Out of the way.
chapters.narration: Here is the wedge build with its points facing outward. The paired members leave a channel along the seams, and those seams connect around the shell. Supply pipes and wiring could run up from the center, then follow accessible channels along the outside skin. Latched in place, out of the way, and still reachable when something changes. Now my dome is looking like a Brainiac build. That fits. The first one was the Frankendome, a conglomerate of different strut types. Apparently I have a theme.

chapters.title: A place for the panels to seat
chapters.promise: The outward wedge leaves a tapered opening.
chapters.narration: The same orientation also gives the panel opening a taper. A slanted edge on a face panel seats against that shape, with a lip to stop it falling through. That is the direction I want to take the frame: removable panels, accessible channels, and attachments that can be improved without throwing the skeleton away.

chapters.title: The pad is the floor
chapters.promise: Bring your home. Bring your carpet if you want it.
chapters.narration: The arriving dome does not bring a second foundation. The deck it lands on is the deck it lives on. Services come through the middle, with an optional utility column for a sink, shower, toilet, and outlets. Bringing the carpet is up to the dome owner. I would. I love carpet. Some people want a garage-shop floor in their house. I have seen it. It works. When the home leaves, the reusable pad remains for the next one. We already see dome rentals, often glorified tents rented a weekend at a time. But own your glorified tent and rent the place to put it, and now both sides have a reason to make a long-term arrangement work. Renting a house has never felt like a way forward to me. A dome is my way out. If I can bring people along with me, that is the point.

chapters.title: Start with the cheapest working version
chapters.promise: A small serviced deck, before the deluxe extras.
chapters.narration: Before the fancy foundation, calculate the starting point. A small framed deck on precast blocks. A fixed rim. One shared power panel and water manifold serving four pads, with a short spur to each. Here is the calculation, line by line, using the current model's working prices. I have kept a site allowance in it, because roads, trunk services, and drainage do not become free just because four people share them. That puts this version above my ten thousand dollar target. It tells me where the design work has to go. It does not justify pretending the difference is gone.

20 ft pad = 314 sq ft
deck on blocks, 314 sq ft: $4,398
share of one hub panel, 1 of 4: $600
spur from the hub: $450
permits: $1,200
site access + trunk service allowance: $6,500
Author's all-in target: $10,000
Fixed rim; shared services; no iris or rotation.
Site allowance must cover the actual local works.
Start with a working floor and services; add features later.

chapters.title: What would a ten-thousand-dollar pad return?
chapters.promise: The target, tested at three proposed rents.
chapters.narration: If I can build a complete serviced pad around ten thousand dollars, what happens at five hundred, a thousand, or fifteen hundred a month? This screen applies the model's occupancy, management, tax, and insurance allowances. At the high end, the target can pay back inside a year. At the low end it takes longer. That is conditional arithmetic. I still have to achieve the build cost and the rent, cover the remaining operating costs, and prove the pad's durability. My aim is infrastructure that serves for ten years and beyond.
equations: WHAT IF the complete pad costs $10,000?

Leased 80% of the year
Management + tax + insurance: $920/year
Utility resale profit assumed zero here.

One-year payback is a scenario, not a promise.

chapters.title: What the host maintains
chapters.promise: The pad and the services. A shorter repair list.
chapters.narration: Look at the host's list: deck, rim, connections, perhaps a meter, perhaps a utility column. Weather and ordinary wear still matter. But there is no tenant-owned kitchen for the host to replace, no sofa to reupholster, and no houseful of furnishings to renew at every turnover. That is the passive-income appeal: a smaller maintenance scope and a longer stay, so the work is concentrated in the infrastructure. Utility metering can be a feature. So can shared off-grid power and water storage serving a cluster. Those are options. The basic income is the pad lease.

chapters.title: The comparison a host actually makes
chapters.promise: Fewer recurring household costs.
chapters.narration: If the alternative is an existing furnished short let, compare the ongoing bills. The model carries the same base management, tax, and insurance allowance on both sides. The short let adds turnover cleaning, a damage reserve, platform fees, and renovation. That is the recurring work a pad host is trying to avoid. This comparison assumes the rental building already exists. Furnishing an existing place is not the same as buying or building a new one.

Short-let operating total: $6,441/year

Renovation allowance: $2,200/year
Existing furnished building assumed; acquisition is excluded.
Pad/deck and service maintenance still need provision.
A smaller maintenance scope; not zero work or zero risk.

chapters.title: Now show the deluxe price
chapters.promise: Rotation, adjustable iris, utility column, and solar.
chapters.narration: Now bring back the deluxe pad: larger concrete deck, rotating base, plumbing column, and an array. Add the adjustable iris separately, because it is another mechanism with another bill. This costs much more than the starter. It can also cost more than furnishing an existing rental. That is a comparison between different starting points and different feature sets. The basic case is a floor and services. A house that turns toward a sunrise is a future option, not the minimum ticket into this system.

A larger pad with rotation, column and solar.
Optional future build; outside the first-site campaign scope.

chapters.title: The work I want to do
chapters.promise: Design the pads. Make the next site repeatable.
chapters.narration: I see my role becoming pad design and getting hosts started. A repeatable foundation and connection standard, with room for hosts to offer different features. Floor heating, water storage, deep freezer storage, a concrete shop floor, rotation, sun tracking, and eventually smart-system brains. Those can become development branches. The first job is to make the simple version work well enough that another host can build it from a clear plan.

chapters.title: The part you can leave to the site
chapters.promise: The same home. A different arrangement underneath.
chapters.narration: On the left is a dome standing on its own foundation. On the right, a home placed on a serviced pad, with its separate foundation removed because the site already provides it. The pad is doing a job you would otherwise have to arrange yourself. That is what lets the portable home concentrate on the parts you can keep and carry.

chapters.title: What a stay costs
chapters.promise: One model. Utilities included on every line.
chapters.narration: Here is the comparison a person actually makes: hotel, short let, apartment, or your own dome on a pad. These are working scenarios, with power and water included on every line. The dome carries upkeep and the cost of tying up money in the house. It also takes a fifteen percent secondhand haircut in this model. You might build your dream home, but only you value every personal choice at the full price you paid. Under these inputs, the dome is cheaper over a year, and you still own it. Change the local rates, and the answer can change too.

and water, because two of them include it in the nightly rate
and dropping it from the other two would rig the compare.

chapters.title: Too long to be a guest
chapters.promise: Too uncertain to sign for a year.
chapters.narration: Run the same options over different stay lengths, and find the point where ownership starts making sense under those inputs. Nobody should buy and move a home just to stay somewhere for a month. A hotel or short let can be exactly the right answer. I am aiming for people who need a place for a while: too long to be a guest, too uncertain to sign for a year. That gap is the whole reason for this system.

nobody should buy a house to stay somewhere for a month.
it starts working at month 3 and never stops. that is the stay length neither a hotel nor a lease serves

chapters.title: What this would have meant to me
chapters.promise: A stable home before the next big step.
chapters.narration: When I was nineteen, I could borrow five grand against my name for college. I blew that opportunity, joined the military, and now at thirty-two I am back for revenge. Constructive revenge, apparently involving domes. I did not fail because I was stupid. My living situation was unstable. I did not have the support I needed, and I could not focus on what mattered. It cost me tremendously. What would a small home I owned have done for my eighteen-year-old self? I think it would have been revolutionary. That is the person I keep in mind when I design this.

chapters.title: Built with the little guy in mind
chapters.promise: Students. Single parents. New families. People starting over.
chapters.narration: Rich people will find ways to have what they want. I want to make a difference for the little guy: single mothers, people with limited money, starting families, bachelors, and people trying to get stable. My mother was a poor single parent. She worked so much that I went to both the before-school program and the after-school program. I wish she had had an economical home system that worked for her, instead of one more thing consuming her life. If there are women with the means to fund something like this, that is who I would especially love to reach. Help me build the kind of stability my mother deserved. I would love to become successful enough to give domes away. Maybe by then I am making dome furniture too. That is an ambition. The first step is a home people can afford to start with and improve.

chapters.title: Semi-nomadic
chapters.promise: Move when it is worth the effort.
chapters.narration: Semi-nomadic means a house that comes apart, not a caravan you tow away on a whim. My working estimate is two days at the quick end, up to two weeks for something large or heavily layered. That is a burst of work: disassemble, transport, reassemble, connect. You spend that effort when a move is worth it. The rest of the time, you are living in a house. A different park, city, or state becomes possible without leaving the house behind. Site agreements still matter, but the improvements to your home travel with you.

chapters.title: The same design, scaled
chapters.promise: Part counts stay fixed. Materials grow with the house.
chapters.narration: Take this design and change only its radius. The small version is about three hundred square feet. The largest here is about two thousand. The model keeps the same counts of struts, hubs, and panels. Its hardware bill stays the same, while the stick lengths and skin area grow. That illustrates the opportunity. It does not prove a connector rated for the small house can hold up the large one. The hardware has to be qualified for the whole intended size and load range first.

the radius. every other menu is held where it was.
19.7 ft  ·     295 sq ft  ·  165 struts  ·  61 hubs  ·  105 panels
32.8 ft  ·     819 sq ft  ·  165 struts  ·  61 hubs  ·  105 panels
52.5 ft  ·   2,096 sq ft  ·  165 struts  ·  61 hubs  ·  105 panels
the counts do not move. the hub bill does not move either:
$596 at 20 ft and $596 at 52 ft.
what moves is the stick and the skin -- panels go from
$1,161 to $8,253, because those are priced by area.
7.1 times the floor off the same list of parts.
that is what makes one good hardware set worth buying: it is the part of the house that does not change when the house does

chapters.title: Buy for the next two steps
chapters.promise: Keep the hardware. Collect the longer members.
chapters.narration: For my wedge system, the plan is to start with a six-foot long member, then move to ten feet, then twelve: roughly twelve hundred square feet at that final target size. This is the one hundred and twenty member wedge frame, a different layout from the catalogue example we just scaled. Keep the qualified connectors and gradually collect the longer pieces for the next build. The skin, insulation, and available pad area have to grow too. Go beyond the planned span and we may change the hardware or increase the dome frequency. That is why I would put money into a good hardware set. It should remain useful across a planned range of builds.
equations: HARDWARE DESIGN BRIEF / size for two upgrades
6 ft longest member -> ~314 sq ft
10 ft longest member -> ~822 sq ft
12 ft longest member -> ~1,184 sq ft
These are the author's target sizes, not a load rating.
Keep qualified connectors; collect longer replacement members.
Larger frames also need more skin, insulation and pad area.
Beyond the rated span, change hardware or frequency.
One purchase should support a planned range of future homes.

chapters.title: A lesson from the Arctic
chapters.promise: Layers under a removable weather shell.
chapters.narration: Some of my own practices make their way into these domes. I stood lookout outside the skin of a ship in the Arctic Circle, for hours at a time, over months. Layers on layers on layers, then a wind-breaking, watertight suit over the whole thing. You look like the Michelin man. You also stay alive. Okay, it was not that dramatic every day. A removable dome shell lets us think similarly: lift the shell, add a suitable quilted layer, potentially using recycled fabric, and put the weather shell back over it. The insulation does not have to stay at whatever level you could afford on the day you built the house.

chapters.title: Improve it over time
chapters.promise: Add insulation when you are ready.
chapters.narration: Here is the model's R-value ladder. Each suitable layer adds thermal resistance, reducing heat transfer through that part of the envelope. The improvement comes from adding the layer, not from the house getting older. You can keep improving heating and cooling performance as you can afford to upgrade. The outer shell still has a separate job: manage weather and wind. A real assembly needs to handle moisture and fire as well. The point is the ability to improve it, rather than treating the first build as the final one.
equations: REMOVABLE SHELL / upgrade the insulation over time
Model assumption: +R-1.6 per quilted layer
0 added layers -> R-1.5
1 added layers -> R-3.1
2 added layers -> R-4.7
3 added layers -> R-6.3
4 added layers -> R-7.9
5 added layers -> R-9.5
6 added layers -> R-11.1
7 added layers -> R-12.7
Actual assemblies need tested moisture and fire performance.
The outer shell supplies the weather and wind barrier.
Insulation improves when you add suitable layers; age alone adds none.

chapters.title: How much shell can carry solar?
chapters.promise: One side. Top half. Whole shell.
chapters.narration: For solar, compare the same twenty-foot-wide dome three ways. Cells on one side. Cells on the top half with a metal skirt below. Or cells over the whole shell. The one-sided version gives rotation the clearest purpose: turn the useful face toward the sun. Whole-shell coverage means some cells face many different directions, so panel area alone cannot tell you the day's energy output. The metal skirt is also a possible rain-catching surface. The choice is about how you want to use the shell.

chapters.title: The size sets a limit
chapters.promise: Capacity from panel area. Output depends on the site.
chapters.narration: Here are the relative capacities, using the measured face area and the model's declared panel density. No panels means zero. The chosen layouts run from about five to ten kilowatts of nameplate capacity on this size dome. Those are installed-capacity figures, not a promise of energy from every curved face. Sun angle, shading, weather, and electrical losses determine production. A larger shell has more area to work with. A communal site could plan around shared demand and storage. That is a useful reason for some hosts to develop a shared energy system.

Panel areas are measured from the model's faces.
Assumed panel density: 18.0 W/sq ft
one side: 292 sq ft -> 5.2 kW
top half, skirt below: 292 sq ft -> 5.2 kW
whole shell: 583 sq ft -> 10.5 kW
No panels = zero installed solar capacity.
Selected layouts: 5.2 to 10.5 kW nameplate.
Face area sets capacity, not guaranteed energy yield.
Sun angle, shade, climate and losses set actual kWh.
The useful limit is the available shell area.

chapters.title: What a site can share
chapters.promise: A bathhouse. A utility core. A choice of services.
chapters.narration: Some hosts can build around communal services. A bathhouse means a small dome may not need its own bathroom. An on-pad utility column is another option: sink, shower, toilet, outlets, and drain at the known connection point. Metered utility resale is optional. Passing through the cost is another approach. A shared off-grid plant with central storage is a more ambitious version. The useful competition between sites is their location, price, services, and how well the arrangement works for the people living there.

chapters.title: Another possible use
chapters.promise: A climate-controlled storage dome.
chapters.narration: A side thought: I can also imagine these as air-conditioned storage buildings. A compact shell, suitable insulation, and a reusable pad could make an interesting storage system. It would need its own performance and cost check, but housing is not the only use for the same kit of parts.

chapters.title: Why a network matters
chapters.promise: More places to go. More people who can use the system.
chapters.narration: The closest comparison is an RV park, with a longer clock. Dome moves take work, so this is aimed at seasons and years rather than a constant stream of overnight stops. One host is a beginning. A second, a third, and eventually hundreds give the dome owner choices and give hosts a pool of residents beyond whoever happens to be in town. That network could also make resale easier. A house you can sell is an asset. A house nobody wants to buy is an expensive tent. I want to build demand for the actual system, not assume it already exists.

chapters.title: Small scale. Small risk.
chapters.promise: Prove a small site, then make it repeatable.
chapters.narration: The goal is a hundred thousand dollars. The land and somewhere to work are already mine, so the campaign can focus on the next practical steps. One to three pads as a test group, and one to three dome designs built and measured. Develop the pad architecture so the next site starts with a plan and a cut list, instead of another invention. Most of the work is modular design and the means to do it: woodworking and metalworking, CNC plasma, three-D printers, a router or mill, casting materials, and the tools to panelize the frame I already have. Then the web app, hosting, documentation, a camera, and real promotion. I want this idea to spread like the flu, instead of sitting in a repository. This is a small pilot, not a claim that all the engineering is finished. The rotating tracking foundation stays outside this first campaign's funded scope. I intend to develop it later.

chapters.title: What supporters get
chapters.promise: Founder status. A signed book. Help shaping your own build.
chapters.narration: What do people get? The entry-level ideas are founder status on an online account, a three-D printed dome keychain or mirror hanger, a window decal, and a poster. A middle tier includes a signed book that goes alongside this codebase, the campaign, and the whole dome approach. At a higher tier, work with me to imagine your own dome, build it digitally, and form a game plan. That could be a future pad host, a dome owner, or somebody collecting possibilities for later. Those are the proposed reward categories. The campaign will set the actual tiers and delivery scope.

chapters.title: Bring your own dome
chapters.promise: Keep the value of the home you improve.
chapters.narration: A hotel sells you a night. A short let sells you a few weeks. A lease sells you a year. I want another option: live somewhere for a while, without handing over every improvement you make to somebody else's building. Bring your own home. Pay the host for the ground and services. Improve your house because it is your house, then take those improvements with you. The source, the model inputs, and the experiments should be open. Actual open source, not just a marketing word. The drawings, the prices, and the things that fail should all be available to check. And if this campaign does not fund, my plan and my work are the same. I am building this whether it takes one year or ten. Support changes the speed and how many people the work reaches along the way.

chapters.title: One person who can carry it further
chapters.promise: Send this to someone who should see it.
chapters.narration: If this was worth your time, send it to one person who can carry it further than I can. A share from somebody with reach can do more for this than a month of me in a field with a chainsaw. That is the ask. Help the idea reach the people who could build it, host it, or need it.

chapters.title: Follow the experiments
chapters.promise: Follow the experiments.
chapters.narration: Everything is documented, including the parts that failed. Instagram, Donovan Zeanah. Facebook dot com slash zeanah. TikTok, short circuiter five. GitHub dot com slash d k zeanah. Zeanah Lab dot com and a Kickstarter for Frankendome are both coming soon.

chapters.title: A home you keep
chapters.promise: BRING YOUR OWN DOME
chapters.narration: Bring your own dome. Build a home. Improve it. Take it with you.

chapters.title: An RV park, for houses
chapters.promise: Serviced pads. You bring the home.
chapters.narration: Think of it as a fancier trailer park. Or maybe better: a stationary RV park, where the thing you park is a house you built and can take apart again.

chapters.title: Why would someone host a dome?
chapters.promise: Passive income, without the rental maintenance.
chapters.narration: So why would people want to host these things? Passive income. Income from land, without the infrastructural maintenance that comes with rental homes. We know the pains of landlords. We know the pains of tenants. I want to bridge the two of them, so that both sides love the arrangement, and each other. That is the dream, anyway.

chapters.title: The pad, and the house that lands on it
chapters.promise: A landowner builds the pad. A dome owner plugs in.
chapters.narration: A landowner builds a circular service pad. A dome owner arrives with their home, sets it down on the pad, and plugs in.

chapters.title: Two people, two colours, one line
chapters.promise: Amber is the pad. Cyan is the house.
chapters.narration: Everything you are about to see is drawn by the Dome Creator's own renderer, and every number comes off the same model the tool uses. There are two people in this network and they want opposite things, so this film keeps them in different colours the whole way through. Amber is the pad host: the deck, the trench, the pedestal, the meter. Cyan is the dome owner: the house, and everything they ever do to it. The single most important thing about that line is that it never moves. The host never owns a building somebody else is living in, and the tenant never pays rent on something that will never be theirs. Which means both sides keep control of their own half. Fewer things to argue about, because there are fewer things held in common. And an easy goodbye, which is worth more than people think: if it is not working, the dome leaves, and the pad is exactly as it was.

chapters.title: A side thought
chapters.promise: Domes make good climate-controlled storage.
chapters.narration: A sidenote. I think domes make great air-conditioned storage. A compact shell leans on the same efficient heating and cooling principles the houses do, and the pad underneath it is already there. It would need its own performance and cost check, and it is not the business this film is about. But housing is not the only thing the same kit of parts can do.

chapters.title: The reserved spot
chapters.promise: Utilities in the centre. Choices around them.
chapters.narration: Pads have their service in the middle. That is the spot every dome builder knows is reserved for the utility station. It is not the only way to do it. It is the only way I will do it. Everything in the dome is reachable from a service point at the centre, and that is what makes the space movable. The partitioning can change without the plumbing having to move with it.

chapters.title: Your life changes. The rooms can too.
chapters.promise: Bedroom, then office, then bedroom again.
chapters.narration: Split a large bedroom to make an office. Three years later you retire, stop needing the office, and open the bedroom back up. I live in a trailer. Four bedrooms, a living room, a den, an office, two bathrooms, a kitchen and a dining area. We have all the allotments of a domicile. But much of that space could be reallocated more efficiently, because the way we need it changed over time. I was gone for six years. I came back. Three people became four, and eventually the same house will be too much for one person. The dome does not have that problem. The shell stays. The room plan can change.

chapters.title: Watch one get built
chapters.promise: Grade, deck, rim, services.
chapters.narration: Change a number in the model and every figure after it moves, because the film reads the table rather than repeating it. So what is a pad? Watch one get built. Grade the ground. Then a deck: gravel, concrete or timber, whatever the host wants to pay for. Then an acceptor rim around the edge. That rim is the part a dome latches to, and it is the reason this is a pad rather than a patio.

chapters.title: Whatever the host wants to pay for
chapters.promise: Gravel, concrete, timber.
chapters.narration: The deck is most of what a pad costs, and it is priced by area, so it is priced by diameter squared. Gravel is the cheapest surface that is still a floor. Concrete is the slab a contractor pours. Timber is the deck a carpenter builds. Everything else on the pad is roughly fixed: the hookups, the permits, and the road that had to reach the site in the first place.

chapters.title: One pad. More than one dome size.
chapters.promise: An iris, with leaves you can watch move.
chapters.narration: That rim is not a fixed ring. It is an iris, on a track, with leaves that open and close like a camera aperture. Watch the contact points move inward, then outward. So one pad takes a twenty foot dome or a forty foot one without being rebuilt. That is the whole reason a host can serve a range of domes with a single piece of hardware. The mechanism is a development concept, and it belongs in the upgrade column.

chapters.title: The deluxe version
chapters.promise: A foundation that turns the house to face what you want.
chapters.narration: Then there is the top-line version: a rotating foundation, with the tracking built into it. This is the expensive one. And honestly, it is just freaking cool. Imagine some days I want the window looking out on the street or the highway. Some days I have someone over, and I want it facing the back corner of the lot instead, where the fence is high. Imagine I have no solar panels at all. Maybe I like the sun in my face in the morning. Maybe I get tired of that and want the opposite, so I face away from it entirely. I imagine there is a lot to be gained from a rotational house in that manner, and more again with panels covering certain parts of the shell asymmetrically. But the bearing, the drive and the rotating utility connections all need their own design. This is future deluxe hardware, at deluxe pricing.

chapters.title: The wedge dome's service channels
chapters.promise: Up the centre. Along the shell. Out of the way.
chapters.narration: Here is the wedge build with its points facing outward. The paired members leave a channel along every seam, and those seams connect around the whole shell. The same orientation gives a panel area with a lip, so a slanted face panel can seat against it and stop where it should.

chapters.title: A place for the panels to seat
chapters.promise: The outward wedge leaves a tapered opening.
chapters.narration: That is the direction I want to take the frame: removable panels, accessible channels, and attachments that can be improved without throwing the skeleton away.

chapters.title: Veins along the outside skin
chapters.promise: From the centre, up, and then out.
chapters.narration: Power, water and drain arrive in the centre. Centre, not edge. From there the runs can go upwards, and then out and into the edge areas, almost like veins along the outside skin of the dome. Latched in place. Out of the way, accessible, and semi-permanent. Which means my dome is now looking like a Brainiac build. That fits, considering the first model I called the Frankendome, a conglomerate of strut types. Apparently I have a theme.

chapters.title: The pad is the floor
chapters.promise: No foundation. No slab. Nothing left behind.
chapters.narration: The dome that lands here puts its floor on the pad. So the services have to come up inside the footprint, or they cross the doorway. A utility column if the host wants one: toilet, sink, shower head, outlets, and a meter pedestal at the rim. The dome that arrives does not bring a foundation, because it does not need one. The pad is the floor. The deck it lands on is the deck it lives on. Bringing the carpet is up to the dome owner. I would. I love carpet. Some people want a garage-shop floor through the whole house. I have seen it. It works. When the owner leaves, the pad is exactly as it was. No slab to break out, no footing to dig up, no permit pulled for a structure that will be gone in a year. We already see dome rentals. They are cheaper to build than a house, and most glamping domes are, let us be honest, glorified tents. I do not think their value ever gets realized by renting them out a weekend at a time. But if a person owned their glorified tent and rented the space to put it on instead, now we are talking. Now both sides get something, and both sides are geared for a long-term exchange of service. Renting a house has never been a way forward for me. Buy-here-pay-here anything is for people with no choice but to be used as pawns by the banking system. A dome is the way out. It is my way out, at the very least. If I can bring people along with me, my job here is done.

chapters.title: The pad catalogue
chapters.promise: Sizes are not invented. They are rounded up.
chapters.narration: Pads come in sizes, and the sizes are not invented. Every design the Dome Creator ships has a foundation diameter, and the tool computes it from its own geometry. Round each one up to the next four feet and you have the pad catalog. Four foot steps, because decking and ring stock come in even lengths, and because the second pad a host builds wants the first one's cut list. Add a bigger dome to the tool, and a bigger pad size appears here on the next run. Nobody edits a list.

chapters.title: What the host actually owns
chapters.promise: A deck, a rim, three pipes and a conduit.
chapters.narration: Look at what the host owns here, because it is a short list. A deck, a rim, three pipes and a conduit, a pedestal with a meter in it, maybe a ring and a column. And it does not have to be poured. There is no kitchen to replace. No sofa to re-upholster. No flooring to pull up because a ten-inch dog lived on it. The host asset is a piece of civil engineering, and the thing most likely to damage it is weather.

chapters.title: Start with the cheapest working version
chapters.promise: A small serviced deck, before the deluxe extras.
chapters.narration: The cheapest version that is still a service pad is a frame deck on pre-cast blocks, with one power panel and a water manifold in the middle of four domes, instead of a pedestal and a trench for each. Nothing excavated, nothing poured. Here is the build cost, line by line, for the smallest pad that takes a real house. Note the two lines that are usually missing from a pitch like this. Site infrastructure: something had to bring a road, a water main and a service drop to this spot, and that cost is real whether or not you count it. And permits. That puts this version above my ten thousand dollar target. It tells me where the design work has to go. It does not justify pretending the difference is gone.
