chapters.title: What would a ten-thousand-dollar pad return?
chapters.promise: The target, tested at three proposed rents.
chapters.narration: If I can make pads at or around a ten thousand dollar build-out, with the water and electrical tie-ins included, it could immediately be rented to a dome owner for what? Five hundred, a thousand, fifteen hundred a month. At the high end it pays itself back inside a year, no contest. And there is nothing there to degrade to begin with, so it is easily a ten-year-plus infrastructural commodity. On the income side the lease is most of it. The utility margin is a cent or two a unit, and that is payment for metering and paperwork rather than a second rent. Here it comes to about ten dollars a month. And payback is on net, after management, tax and insurance. Payback on gross is a brochure number.

Utility resale profit assumed zero here.

chapters.title: Below the line and above it
chapters.promise: The host's money is in the ground. The tenant's goes with them.
chapters.narration: Two people, one pad, and a line between them that does not move. Below the line is the host's money, and it is in the ground. Above the line is the tenant's money, and it is a drive away with them. That is the arrangement, and it is the opposite of every other way people rent somewhere to live. A landlord's money is in the walls the tenant is living between. That is where the conflict comes from, every time.

chapters.title: The comparison a host actually makes
chapters.promise: Fewer recurring household costs.
chapters.narration: The honest comparison for a landowner is not against nothing. It is against furnishing a place and letting it out, which is what most people with a spare building actually do. So both columns carry the same management, the same tax, the same insurance. The short-let scenario of renting by the building then adds cleaning at every turnover, a damage reserve, a platform fee and a renovation cycle. Several times the pad host's yearly bill, forever. A dome pad is a truly passive income asset.

chapters.title: The work I want to do
chapters.promise: Design the pads. Make the next site repeatable.
chapters.narration: My eventual business, the role I will inevitably fill, is pad design and initializing for hosts. Unique feature sets can go here. Floor heating. Built-in water storage. Built-in deep-freeze storage. Rotation and sun tracking. A concrete shop floor, ready to work on. And eventually the computer and smart-system brains, which is for later. The first job is to make the simple version work well enough that another host can build it from a clear plan.

chapters.title: Now show the deluxe price
chapters.promise: Rotation, adjustable iris, utility column, and solar.
chapters.narration: And now the figure that does not help us. A loaded pad, rotating, plumbed, carrying an array, costs more upfront than a bare pad with a furnished let on it. On day one, the short-let house rental wins. The pad host case was never that it is cheaper to start. It is that none of their yearly bill is where a building somebody else is living in.

chapters.title: The part you can leave to the site
chapters.promise: The same home. A different arrangement underneath.
chapters.narration: Now the tenant side, and it starts underground. On the left, the design as the Dome Creator ships it, standing on its own foundation. On the right, the same design on a pad, with that foundation taken out from under it, because the pad is already there. Same house. The difference is the ground, and the ground is the one part of a building you can never take with you when you go.

chapters.title: What a stay costs
chapters.promise: One model. Utilities included on every line.
chapters.narration: Here is the comparison a person actually makes, priced on one basis, so it is a fair one. Every line carries power and water, because two of them include it in the nightly rate, and quietly dropping it from the other two would rig the result. The dome line carries the two costs an ownership pitch usually hides: upkeep, and the return the money would have made if it were not sitting in a house. And it is worth less the day after you buy it, so a secondhand haircut comes off on day one. Pay to build your dream home and only you value every personal choice at the full price you paid. So fifteen percent comes off that just to start the negotiation. Even carrying all of that, a year in your own dome on a pad costs less than a year in the cheapest thing you could rent. And at the end of it you still own a house.

chapters.title: Too long to be a guest
chapters.promise: Too uncertain to sign for a year.
chapters.narration: So how long does the stay have to be? Run those same four options at every length, and find the month the dome stops being the expensive answer. Nobody should buy a house to stay somewhere for a month. Under that line a short let is the right answer, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. Past it, the gap opens and never closes. Most people fit in the categories this is aimed at: too long to be a guest, too uncertain to sign for a year. That is the part of the market neither a hotel nor a twelve month lease has ever served.

chapters.title: What this would have meant to me
chapters.promise: A stable home before the next big step.
chapters.narration: When I was nineteen I was able to borrow five grand against my name, for college. I blew that, joined the military, and now at thirty-two I am back for revenge. Constructive revenge, apparently involving domes. I did not fail out because I was stupid. I had no overarching support, I was not stable in my living situations, and I could not focus on the thing that mattered in that time: school. It cost me greatly. Tremendously, if you ask me. What a dome would have done for my eighteen-year-old self would have been revolutionary. That is how I am designing this, and going forward.

chapters.title: Built with the little guy in mind
chapters.promise: Students. Single parents. New families.
chapters.narration: I think college-aged students would get three times the investment out of a dome system than out of a squandered semester. A realistic five thousand dollar dome home is doable, especially when you rely on the pad for the essentials. The trailer model of the dome world, so to speak. Rich people will find their own way to have what they want without me. The small people, that is who I can impact. Single mothers. The economically vulnerable. Starting families. Bachelors. My mother was a poor single parent. She worked so much that I went to the before-school program and the after-school program on the same day. I wish she had had a stable, economical home system that worked for her and made sense. I would love to be so successful that I can give away domes. Maybe by then I am making dome furniture too. That is an ambition. The first step is a home people can afford to start with and improve.

chapters.title: Semi-nomadic
chapters.promise: Move when it is worth the effort.
chapters.narration: The word that describes the whole idea is semi-nomadic. Not a caravan you tow away on a whim. A house that comes apart: two days at the quick end, two weeks for something large or heavily layered. That is a real burst of effort, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But it is a burst, not a condition. You spend it when a move is worth it, and the rest of the time you are simply living in a house. Off one pad and onto another. A different park, a different city, a different state. No lease broken, no deposit argued over, no walkthrough with somebody's clipboard. Nothing left behind, and every improvement the owner has ever made goes with them. The money they spent is still theirs, standing on the next pad.

chapters.title: The same design, scaled
chapters.promise: Part counts stay fixed. Materials grow with the house.
chapters.narration: Take one design and move a single slider: the radius. Everything else is held exactly where it was. Twenty feet across, thirty-three feet across, fifty-two feet across. Two hundred and ninety-five square feet up to two thousand and ninety-six. And the part list on the bench in front of you never changes. The counts are identical across all three. The same struts, the same hubs, the same panels. And the hub bill is identical to the same dollars at twenty feet as it is at fifty-two. What does move is the stick and the skin, because those are priced by the meter and the square meter. Seven times the floor off the same list of parts. The hardware is a range of sizes, shipped with two sizes up in mind as the base level. That is what makes one good hardware set worth paying for: it is the part of the house that does not change when the house does, so it is the part you buy once and keep.

chapters.title: Buy for the next two steps
chapters.promise: Keep the hardware. Collect the longer members.
chapters.narration: Pads come in sizes, and so does the hardware. Start with the base model and size it two steps ahead. For my wedge system the plan is to start with a six foot long member, go to ten feet, then twelve: about twelve hundred square feet at that final target size. Any bigger, and we start upping the dome frequency. Sinking capital into the hardware majority is the advantage, because that is the part that remains and gets reused when a bigger dome is wanted. The longer members get collected gradually, on the way. That is why I would put money into a good hardware set: it should remain useful across a planned range of builds.

6 ft longest member -> ~314 sq ft

chapters.title: A lesson from the Arctic
chapters.promise: Layers under a removable weather shell.
chapters.narration: Some of my own practices make their way into these domes. I stood lookout outside the skin of a ship in the Arctic Circle, for hours at a time, over months. There is exactly one way to stay warm out there: layers on layers on layers, and then a wind-breaking, watertight suit over all of it. You end up looking like the Michelin man. You also stay alive. It was not that bad. A dome with a removable shell can work the same way. Lift the shell, add a quilted layer, put the shell back over it. Quilted recycled fabric is one of the largest waste streams there is.

chapters.title: Improve it over time
chapters.promise: The number keeps going up for as long as you own it.
chapters.narration: Which means our value stops being a number somebody decided on the day the house was built. The R-value is not a static figure. It can keep going up for as long as you own the house: better at heating and better at cooling, year after year, because you added the layer that was worth adding that year. Two honest limits. Seven layers is a good wall, not a code-beating one. And this prices conduction only. It does not price the windbreak, and the windbreak is what makes layers work. That is the shell's job, and it is the part of the Arctic argument this model cannot check.
equations: REMOVABLE SHELL / upgrade the insulation over time
Model assumption: +R-1.6 per quilted layer
0 added layers -> R-1.5
1 added layers -> R-3.1
2 added layers -> R-4.7
3 added layers -> R-6.3
4 added layers -> R-7.9
5 added layers -> R-9.5
6 added layers -> R-11.1
7 added layers -> R-12.7
Actual assemblies need tested moisture and fire performance.
The outer shell supplies the weather and wind barrier.

chapters.title: How much shell can carry solar?
chapters.promise: One side. Top half. Whole shell.
chapters.narration: A pad on a rotating base can aim whatever is standing on it. The dome in this chapter is a ten foot radius shell, the medium two-person size, because kilowatt hours a month mean nothing without the dome they came off. Three ways to clad it. One side, so the pad turns that side to the sun. The top half, with a metal skirt below it, where the skirt is the rain catchment as well as the weather edge. Or the whole shell, which makes the most power and gives you the least reason to turn anything, because something is always facing the sun. Single axis tracking adds about a quarter over a fixed array, and on this dome that is several hundred kilowatt hours a month.

chapters.title: The size sets a limit
chapters.promise: Capacity from panel area. Output depends on the site.
chapters.narration: Here are the relative capacities, using the measured face area and the model's declared panel density. The limit is the shell area: at this size the layouts run from about five to ten kilowatts of nameplate capacity, and a larger shell has more area to work with. But here is the number that first made this model wrong. A dome shell carries far more panel than a household inside it consumes. Several times more. The first version of this model valued every generated kilowatt hour at the retail price, which quietly assumed the tenant was buying power they would never have bought. So it does not any more. What displaces the tenant's own draw is worth retail. Everything past it is worth export, which is about a third of that. Correcting it took this pad's solar income down by well over half. The ring is still worth fitting. But the real case for cladding a dome in cells is a park that can sell the surplus, not a tenant who cannot use it.

Panel areas are measured from the model's faces.
Assumed panel density: 18.0 W/sq ft
one side: 292 sq ft -> 5.2 kW
top half, skirt below: 292 sq ft -> 5.2 kW
whole shell: 583 sq ft -> 10.5 kW
No panels = zero installed solar capacity.
Selected layouts: 5.2 to 10.5 kW nameplate.

chapters.title: What a site can share
chapters.promise: A bathhouse. A utility core. A choice of services.
chapters.narration: Some of this can be shared, and that changes what a dome has to be. A bathhouse on the site means a dome owner can skip plumbing entirely, which is the single most expensive and most regulated thing in a small dwelling. Or the host fits the utility column on the pad, once, for every tenant who ever parks there. Either way it is bought once by the person who owns it, and used by everyone who comes and goes. And note what a host is not obliged to do. Reselling power and water with a margin is one option, not the model. A host may simply pass the meter through. What a host is really competing on is the array of things a site offers, and the price they can ask follows from that.

chapters.title: Why a network matters
chapters.promise: More places to go. More people who can use the system.
chapters.narration: The closest thing that exists is an RV park, and the comparison is worth making carefully. An RV park turns over in nights and weeks. A dome park turns over in seasons and years, because taking a dome down is a job rather than a decision. Same shape of arrangement, much longer clock. One host with one pad is a favor. What makes this worth building is the second host, and the third, and the four hundredth. For the dome owner, a network means choice: price, location, services, and the freedom to leave a bad host by driving away from them. For the pad host, it means a tenant pool that is not limited to whoever happens to be in town, and it means the dome has a resale market, which is the one assumption in this film doing the most work. A house you can sell is an asset. A house nobody will buy is a very expensive tent.

chapters.title: Small scale. Small risk.
chapters.promise: Prove a small site, then make it repeatable.
chapters.narration: The goal is a hundred thousand dollars. I think that is a modest number to strive for, and it is modest because the expensive parts are already mine: the land, and somewhere to work. What the money builds is one to three pads on that land, as a test group, and the pad architecture itself made repeatable, the way RV hookups are repeatable, so the second site is a cut list rather than an invention. Most of it goes into modular design and the means to do it. A full woodworking and metalworking shop. CNC plasma torches, three-D printers, a mill, casting materials, a laser, a router: a lab for panelizing the frame and skeleton I already have realized. One to three dome designs that actually suit this, built and measured. Then the web app and its hosting and promotion. Real advertising on every platform I can reach, because I want this idea to spread like the flu rather than sit in a repository. And a camera, because all of it gets published as it is made. What the campaign does not buy is the tracking foundation. A pad that turns to follow the sun is a fine thing to own and I intend to build one, but it is whimsy on the first site, and I am not spending anyone else's money on it.

chapters.title: What supporters get
chapters.promise: Founder status. A signed book. Help shaping your own build.
chapters.narration: So what do the people get? An online account with founder status, a three-D printed dome model keychain, a rear view mirror hanger, a window decal, a poster. The middle tier adds a signed book that goes along with this codebase, the campaign, and the whole dome paradigm. The high tier gets help idealizing and building digitally with me: game-plan forming for your own dome realization. For future pad owners, dome collectors, and anybody gathering possibilities for later. Those are the proposed categories. The campaign will set the actual tiers and delivery scope.

chapters.title: Bring your own dome
chapters.promise: Keep the value of the home you improve.
chapters.narration: A hotel sells you a night. A short let sells you a fortnight. A lease sells you a year and then charges you to leave early. And a rental home is somebody handing you a money shredder at your convenience, for use on your own stash. One of those sells you the thing most people actually want, which is to live somewhere for a while without handing over the value of everything they do to the place while they are there. Bring your own home. Pay the host for the ground and the services. Improve your house as much as you like, because it is your house, and take every bit of that with you when you go. The source, the model inputs and the experiments should be open. Actual open source, not the kind where the word is doing marketing. The drawings, the prices and the things that fail should all be available to check. Nothing in this film was asserted. Every pad and every dome was drawn by the tool that designs them. Every figure was computed by the model underneath it, and the numbers that argue against this idea are in here with the ones that argue for it. Come and check them.

chapters.title: One person who can carry it further
chapters.promise: Send this to someone who should see it.
chapters.narration: And one last thing, said plainly. If this campaign does not fund, my plan and my work are the same. I am building this whether it takes one year or ten. What a donation changes is the speed, and whether the drawings reach anybody else on the way. If any of this was worth your time, send it to one person who can carry it further than I can. That is the whole ask. One share from somebody with reach does more for this than a month of me in a field with a chainsaw.

chapters.title: Follow the experiments
chapters.promise: Follow the experiments.
chapters.narration: Everything is documented, including the parts that failed. Instagram, Donovan Zeanah. Facebook dot com slash zeanah. TikTok, short circuiter five. GitHub dot com slash d k zeanah. Zeanah Lab dot com and a Kickstarter for Frankendome are both coming soon.

title: Bring Your Own Dome (snarky)
note: Bring Your Own Dome in the social register: handheld camera that leans in when the character speaks, a little faster, vignetted, and the pink cyber jelly on thirteen cues, taking the tone of each passage it stands in. Same script, same numbers, same claims as the deepseek cut.
family_note: a style variant of the same script

chapters.title: A home you keep
chapters.promise: BRING YOUR OWN DOME
chapters.narration: Bring your own dome. Build a home. Improve it. Take it with you.

chapters.title: An RV park, for houses
chapters.promise: Serviced pads. You bring the home.
chapters.narration: Think of it as a fancier trailer park. Or maybe better: a stationary RV park, where the thing you park is a house you built and can take apart again.

chapters.title: Why would someone host a dome?
chapters.promise: Passive income, without the rental maintenance.
chapters.narration: So why would people want to host these things? Passive income. Income from land, without the infrastructural maintenance that comes with rental homes. We know the pains of landlords. We know the pains of tenants. I want to bridge the two of them, so that both sides love the arrangement, and each other. That is the dream, anyway.

chapters.title: The pad, and the house that lands on it
chapters.promise: A landowner builds the pad. A dome owner plugs in.
chapters.narration: A landowner builds a circular service pad. A dome owner arrives with their home, sets it down on the pad, and plugs in.

chapters.title: Two people, two colours, one line
chapters.promise: Amber is the pad. Cyan is the house.
chapters.narration: Everything you are about to see is drawn by the Dome Creator's own renderer, and every number comes off the same model the tool uses. There are two people in this network and they want opposite things, so this film keeps them in different colours the whole way through. Amber is the pad host: the deck, the trench, the pedestal, the meter. Cyan is the dome owner: the house, and everything they ever do to it. The single most important thing about that line is that it never moves. The host never owns a building somebody else is living in, and the tenant never pays rent on something that will never be theirs. Which means both sides keep control of their own half. Fewer things to argue about, because there are fewer things held in common. And an easy goodbye, which is worth more than people think: if it is not working, the dome leaves, and the pad is exactly as it was.

chapters.title: A side thought
chapters.promise: Domes make good climate-controlled storage.
chapters.narration: A sidenote. I think domes make great air-conditioned storage. A compact shell leans on the same efficient heating and cooling principles the houses do, and the pad underneath it is already there. It would need its own performance and cost check, and it is not the business this film is about. But housing is not the only thing the same kit of parts can do.

chapters.title: The reserved spot
chapters.promise: Utilities in the centre. Choices around them.
chapters.narration: Pads have their service in the middle. That is the spot every dome builder knows is reserved for the utility station. It is not the only way to do it. It is the only way I will do it. Everything in the dome is reachable from a service point at the centre, and that is what makes the space movable. The partitioning can change without the plumbing having to move with it.

chapters.title: Your life changes. The rooms can too.
chapters.promise: Bedroom, then office, then bedroom again.
chapters.narration: Split a large bedroom to make an office. Three years later you retire, stop needing the office, and open the bedroom back up. I live in a trailer. Four bedrooms, a living room, a den, an office, two bathrooms, a kitchen and a dining area. We have all the allotments of a domicile. But much of that space could be reallocated more efficiently, because the way we need it changed over time. I was gone for six years. I came back. Three people became four, and eventually the same house will be too much for one person. The dome does not have that problem. The shell stays. The room plan can change.

chapters.title: Watch one get built
chapters.promise: Grade, deck, rim, services.
chapters.narration: Change a number in the model and every figure after it moves, because the film reads the table rather than repeating it. So what is a pad? Watch one get built. Grade the ground. Then a deck: gravel, concrete or timber, whatever the host wants to pay for. Then an acceptor rim around the edge. That rim is the part a dome latches to, and it is the reason this is a pad rather than a patio.

chapters.title: Whatever the host wants to pay for
chapters.promise: Gravel, concrete, timber.
chapters.narration: The deck is most of what a pad costs, and it is priced by area, so it is priced by diameter squared. Gravel is the cheapest surface that is still a floor. Concrete is the slab a contractor pours. Timber is the deck a carpenter builds. Everything else on the pad is roughly fixed: the hookups, the permits, and the road that had to reach the site in the first place.

chapters.title: One pad. More than one dome size.
chapters.promise: An iris, with leaves you can watch move.
chapters.narration: That rim is not a fixed ring. It is an iris, on a track, with leaves that open and close like a camera aperture. Watch the contact points move inward, then outward. So one pad takes a twenty foot dome or a forty foot one without being rebuilt. That is the whole reason a host can serve a range of domes with a single piece of hardware. The mechanism is a development concept, and it belongs in the upgrade column.

chapters.title: The deluxe version
chapters.promise: A foundation that turns the house to face what you want.
chapters.narration: Then there is the top-line version: a rotating foundation, with the tracking built into it. This is the expensive one. And honestly, it is just freaking cool. Imagine some days I want the window looking out on the street or the highway. Some days I have someone over, and I want it facing the back corner of the lot instead, where the fence is high. Imagine I have no solar panels at all. Maybe I like the sun in my face in the morning. Maybe I get tired of that and want the opposite, so I face away from it entirely. I imagine there is a lot to be gained from a rotational house in that manner, and more again with panels covering certain parts of the shell asymmetrically. But the bearing, the drive and the rotating utility connections all need their own design. This is future deluxe hardware, at deluxe pricing.

chapters.title: The wedge dome's service channels
chapters.promise: Up the centre. Along the shell. Out of the way.
chapters.narration: Here is the wedge build with its points facing outward. The paired members leave a channel along every seam, and those seams connect around the whole shell. The same orientation gives a panel area with a lip, so a slanted face panel can seat against it and stop where it should.

chapters.title: A place for the panels to seat
chapters.promise: The outward wedge leaves a tapered opening.
chapters.narration: That is the direction I want to take the frame: removable panels, accessible channels, and attachments that can be improved without throwing the skeleton away.

chapters.title: Veins along the outside skin
chapters.promise: From the centre, up, and then out.
chapters.narration: Power, water and drain arrive in the centre. Centre, not edge. From there the runs can go upwards, and then out and into the edge areas, almost like veins along the outside skin of the dome. Latched in place. Out of the way, accessible, and semi-permanent. Which means my dome is now looking like a Brainiac build. That fits, considering the first model I called the Frankendome, a conglomerate of strut types. Apparently I have a theme.

chapters.title: The pad is the floor
chapters.promise: No foundation. No slab. Nothing left behind.
chapters.narration: The dome that lands here puts its floor on the pad. So the services have to come up inside the footprint, or they cross the doorway. A utility column if the host wants one: toilet, sink, shower head, outlets, and a meter pedestal at the rim. The dome that arrives does not bring a foundation, because it does not need one. The pad is the floor. The deck it lands on is the deck it lives on. Bringing the carpet is up to the dome owner. I would. I love carpet. Some people want a garage-shop floor through the whole house. I have seen it. It works. When the owner leaves, the pad is exactly as it was. No slab to break out, no footing to dig up, no permit pulled for a structure that will be gone in a year. We already see dome rentals. They are cheaper to build than a house, and most glamping domes are, let us be honest, glorified tents. I do not think their value ever gets realized by renting them out a weekend at a time. But if a person owned their glorified tent and rented the space to put it on instead, now we are talking. Now both sides get something, and both sides are geared for a long-term exchange of service. Renting a house has never been a way forward for me. Buy-here-pay-here anything is for people with no choice but to be used as pawns by the banking system. A dome is the way out. It is my way out, at the very least. If I can bring people along with me, my job here is done.

chapters.title: The pad catalogue
chapters.promise: Sizes are not invented. They are rounded up.
chapters.narration: Pads come in sizes, and the sizes are not invented. Every design the Dome Creator ships has a foundation diameter, and the tool computes it from its own geometry. Round each one up to the next four feet and you have the pad catalog. Four foot steps, because decking and ring stock come in even lengths, and because the second pad a host builds wants the first one's cut list. Add a bigger dome to the tool, and a bigger pad size appears here on the next run. Nobody edits a list.

chapters.title: What the host actually owns
chapters.promise: A deck, a rim, three pipes and a conduit.
chapters.narration: Look at what the host owns here, because it is a short list. A deck, a rim, three pipes and a conduit, a pedestal with a meter in it, maybe a ring and a column. And it does not have to be poured. There is no kitchen to replace. No sofa to re-upholster. No flooring to pull up because a ten-inch dog lived on it. The host asset is a piece of civil engineering, and the thing most likely to damage it is weather.

chapters.title: Start with the cheapest working version
chapters.promise: A small serviced deck, before the deluxe extras.
chapters.narration: The cheapest version that is still a service pad is a frame deck on pre-cast blocks, with one power panel and a water manifold in the middle of four domes, instead of a pedestal and a trench for each. Nothing excavated, nothing poured. Here is the build cost, line by line, for the smallest pad that takes a real house. Note the two lines that are usually missing from a pitch like this. Site infrastructure: something had to bring a road, a water main and a service drop to this spot, and that cost is real whether or not you count it. And permits. That puts this version above my ten thousand dollar target. It tells me where the design work has to go. It does not justify pretending the difference is gone.

chapters.title: What would a ten-thousand-dollar pad return?
chapters.promise: The target, tested at three proposed rents.
chapters.narration: If I can make pads at or around a ten thousand dollar build-out, with the water and electrical tie-ins included, it could immediately be rented to a dome owner for what? Five hundred, a thousand, fifteen hundred a month. At the high end it pays itself back inside a year, no contest. And there is nothing there to degrade to begin with, so it is easily a ten-year-plus infrastructural commodity. On the income side the lease is most of it. The utility margin is a cent or two a unit, and that is payment for metering and paperwork rather than a second rent. Here it comes to about ten dollars a month. And payback is on net, after management, tax and insurance. Payback on gross is a brochure number.

chapters.title: Below the line and above it
chapters.promise: The host's money is in the ground. The tenant's goes with them.
chapters.narration: Two people, one pad, and a line between them that does not move. Below the line is the host's money, and it is in the ground. Above the line is the tenant's money, and it is a drive away with them. That is the arrangement, and it is the opposite of every other way people rent somewhere to live. A landlord's money is in the walls the tenant is living between. That is where the conflict comes from, every time.

chapters.title: The comparison a host actually makes
chapters.promise: Fewer recurring household costs.
chapters.narration: The honest comparison for a landowner is not against nothing. It is against furnishing a place and letting it out, which is what most people with a spare building actually do. So both columns carry the same management, the same tax, the same insurance. The short-let scenario of renting by the building then adds cleaning at every turnover, a damage reserve, a platform fee and a renovation cycle. Several times the pad host's yearly bill, forever. A dome pad is a truly passive income asset.

chapters.title: The work I want to do
chapters.promise: Design the pads. Make the next site repeatable.
chapters.narration: My eventual business, the role I will inevitably fill, is pad design and initializing for hosts. Unique feature sets can go here. Floor heating. Built-in water storage. Built-in deep-freeze storage. Rotation and sun tracking. A concrete shop floor, ready to work on. And eventually the computer and smart-system brains, which is for later. The first job is to make the simple version work well enough that another host can build it from a clear plan.

chapters.title: Now show the deluxe price
chapters.promise: Rotation, adjustable iris, utility column, and solar.
chapters.narration: And now the figure that does not help us. A loaded pad, rotating, plumbed, carrying an array, costs more upfront than a bare pad with a furnished let on it. On day one, the short-let house rental wins. The pad host case was never that it is cheaper to start. It is that none of their yearly bill is where a building somebody else is living in.

chapters.title: The part you can leave to the site
chapters.promise: The same home. A different arrangement underneath.
chapters.narration: Now the tenant side, and it starts underground. On the left, the design as the Dome Creator ships it, standing on its own foundation. On the right, the same design on a pad, with that foundation taken out from under it, because the pad is already there. Same house. The difference is the ground, and the ground is the one part of a building you can never take with you when you go.

chapters.title: What a stay costs
chapters.promise: One model. Utilities included on every line.
chapters.narration: Here is the comparison a person actually makes, priced on one basis, so it is a fair one. Every line carries power and water, because two of them include it in the nightly rate, and quietly dropping it from the other two would rig the result. The dome line carries the two costs an ownership pitch usually hides: upkeep, and the return the money would have made if it were not sitting in a house. And it is worth less the day after you buy it, so a secondhand haircut comes off on day one. Pay to build your dream home and only you value every personal choice at the full price you paid. So fifteen percent comes off that just to start the negotiation. Even carrying all of that, a year in your own dome on a pad costs less than a year in the cheapest thing you could rent. And at the end of it you still own a house.

chapters.title: Too long to be a guest
chapters.promise: Too uncertain to sign for a year.
chapters.narration: So how long does the stay have to be? Run those same four options at every length, and find the month the dome stops being the expensive answer. Nobody should buy a house to stay somewhere for a month. Under that line a short let is the right answer, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. Past it, the gap opens and never closes. Most people fit in the categories this is aimed at: too long to be a guest, too uncertain to sign for a year. That is the part of the market neither a hotel nor a twelve month lease has ever served.

chapters.title: What this would have meant to me
chapters.promise: A stable home before the next big step.
chapters.narration: When I was nineteen I was able to borrow five grand against my name, for college. I blew that, joined the military, and now at thirty-two I am back for revenge. Constructive revenge, apparently involving domes. I did not fail out because I was stupid. I had no overarching support, I was not stable in my living situations, and I could not focus on the thing that mattered in that time: school. It cost me greatly. Tremendously, if you ask me. What a dome would have done for my eighteen-year-old self would have been revolutionary. That is how I am designing this, and going forward.

chapters.title: Built with the little guy in mind
chapters.promise: Students. Single parents. New families.
chapters.narration: I think college-aged students would get three times the investment out of a dome system than out of a squandered semester. A realistic five thousand dollar dome home is doable, especially when you rely on the pad for the essentials. The trailer model of the dome world, so to speak. Rich people will find their own way to have what they want without me. The small people, that is who I can impact. Single mothers. The economically vulnerable. Starting families. Bachelors. My mother was a poor single parent. She worked so much that I went to the before-school program and the after-school program on the same day. I wish she had had a stable, economical home system that worked for her and made sense. I would love to be so successful that I can give away domes. Maybe by then I am making dome furniture too. That is an ambition. The first step is a home people can afford to start with and improve.

chapters.title: Semi-nomadic
chapters.promise: Move when it is worth the effort.
chapters.narration: The word that describes the whole idea is semi-nomadic. Not a caravan you tow away on a whim. A house that comes apart: two days at the quick end, two weeks for something large or heavily layered. That is a real burst of effort, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But it is a burst, not a condition. You spend it when a move is worth it, and the rest of the time you are simply living in a house. Off one pad and onto another. A different park, a different city, a different state. No lease broken, no deposit argued over, no walkthrough with somebody's clipboard. Nothing left behind, and every improvement the owner has ever made goes with them. The money they spent is still theirs, standing on the next pad.

chapters.title: The same design, scaled
chapters.promise: Part counts stay fixed. Materials grow with the house.
chapters.narration: Take one design and move a single slider: the radius. Everything else is held exactly where it was. Twenty feet across, thirty-three feet across, fifty-two feet across. Two hundred and ninety-five square feet up to two thousand and ninety-six. And the part list on the bench in front of you never changes. The counts are identical across all three. The same struts, the same hubs, the same panels. And the hub bill is identical to the same dollars at twenty feet as it is at fifty-two. What does move is the stick and the skin, because those are priced by the meter and the square meter. Seven times the floor off the same list of parts. The hardware is a range of sizes, shipped with two sizes up in mind as the base level. That is what makes one good hardware set worth paying for: it is the part of the house that does not change when the house does, so it is the part you buy once and keep.

chapters.title: Buy for the next two steps
chapters.promise: Keep the hardware. Collect the longer members.
chapters.narration: Pads come in sizes, and so does the hardware. Start with the base model and size it two steps ahead. For my wedge system the plan is to start with a six foot long member, go to ten feet, then twelve: about twelve hundred square feet at that final target size. Any bigger, and we start upping the dome frequency. Sinking capital into the hardware majority is the advantage, because that is the part that remains and gets reused when a bigger dome is wanted. The longer members get collected gradually, on the way. That is why I would put money into a good hardware set: it should remain useful across a planned range of builds.

chapters.title: A lesson from the Arctic
chapters.promise: Layers under a removable weather shell.
chapters.narration: Some of my own practices make their way into these domes. I stood lookout outside the skin of a ship in the Arctic Circle, for hours at a time, over months. There is exactly one way to stay warm out there: layers on layers on layers, and then a wind-breaking, watertight suit over all of it. You end up looking like the Michelin man. You also stay alive. It was not that bad. A dome with a removable shell can work the same way. Lift the shell, add a quilted layer, put the shell back over it. Quilted recycled fabric is one of the largest waste streams there is.

chapters.title: Improve it over time
chapters.promise: The number keeps going up for as long as you own it.
chapters.narration: Which means our value stops being a number somebody decided on the day the house was built. The R-value is not a static figure. It can keep going up for as long as you own the house: better at heating and better at cooling, year after year, because you added the layer that was worth adding that year. Two honest limits. Seven layers is a good wall, not a code-beating one. And this prices conduction only. It does not price the windbreak, and the windbreak is what makes layers work. That is the shell's job, and it is the part of the Arctic argument this model cannot check.

chapters.title: How much shell can carry solar?
chapters.promise: One side. Top half. Whole shell.
chapters.narration: A pad on a rotating base can aim whatever is standing on it. The dome in this chapter is a ten foot radius shell, the medium two-person size, because kilowatt hours a month mean nothing without the dome they came off. Three ways to clad it. One side, so the pad turns that side to the sun. The top half, with a metal skirt below it, where the skirt is the rain catchment as well as the weather edge. Or the whole shell, which makes the most power and gives you the least reason to turn anything, because something is always facing the sun. Single axis tracking adds about a quarter over a fixed array, and on this dome that is several hundred kilowatt hours a month.

chapters.title: The size sets a limit
chapters.promise: Capacity from panel area. Output depends on the site.
chapters.narration: Here are the relative capacities, using the measured face area and the model's declared panel density. The limit is the shell area: at this size the layouts run from about five to ten kilowatts of nameplate capacity, and a larger shell has more area to work with. But here is the number that first made this model wrong. A dome shell carries far more panel than a household inside it consumes. Several times more. The first version of this model valued every generated kilowatt hour at the retail price, which quietly assumed the tenant was buying power they would never have bought. So it does not any more. What displaces the tenant's own draw is worth retail. Everything past it is worth export, which is about a third of that. Correcting it took this pad's solar income down by well over half. The ring is still worth fitting. But the real case for cladding a dome in cells is a park that can sell the surplus, not a tenant who cannot use it.

chapters.title: What a site can share
chapters.promise: A bathhouse. A utility core. A choice of services.
chapters.narration: Some of this can be shared, and that changes what a dome has to be. A bathhouse on the site means a dome owner can skip plumbing entirely, which is the single most expensive and most regulated thing in a small dwelling. Or the host fits the utility column on the pad, once, for every tenant who ever parks there. Either way it is bought once by the person who owns it, and used by everyone who comes and goes. And note what a host is not obliged to do. Reselling power and water with a margin is one option, not the model. A host may simply pass the meter through. What a host is really competing on is the array of things a site offers, and the price they can ask follows from that.

chapters.title: Why a network matters
chapters.promise: More places to go. More people who can use the system.
chapters.narration: The closest thing that exists is an RV park, and the comparison is worth making carefully. An RV park turns over in nights and weeks. A dome park turns over in seasons and years, because taking a dome down is a job rather than a decision. Same shape of arrangement, much longer clock. One host with one pad is a favor. What makes this worth building is the second host, and the third, and the four hundredth. For the dome owner, a network means choice: price, location, services, and the freedom to leave a bad host by driving away from them. For the pad host, it means a tenant pool that is not limited to whoever happens to be in town, and it means the dome has a resale market, which is the one assumption in this film doing the most work. A house you can sell is an asset. A house nobody will buy is a very expensive tent.

chapters.title: Small scale. Small risk.
chapters.promise: Prove a small site, then make it repeatable.
chapters.narration: The goal is a hundred thousand dollars. I think that is a modest number to strive for, and it is modest because the expensive parts are already mine: the land, and somewhere to work. What the money builds is one to three pads on that land, as a test group, and the pad architecture itself made repeatable, the way RV hookups are repeatable, so the second site is a cut list rather than an invention. Most of it goes into modular design and the means to do it. A full woodworking and metalworking shop. CNC plasma torches, three-D printers, a mill, casting materials, a laser, a router: a lab for panelizing the frame and skeleton I already have realized. One to three dome designs that actually suit this, built and measured. Then the web app and its hosting and promotion. Real advertising on every platform I can reach, because I want this idea to spread like the flu rather than sit in a repository. And a camera, because all of it gets published as it is made. What the campaign does not buy is the tracking foundation. A pad that turns to follow the sun is a fine thing to own and I intend to build one, but it is whimsy on the first site, and I am not spending anyone else's money on it.

chapters.title: What supporters get
chapters.promise: Founder status. A signed book. Help shaping your own build.
chapters.narration: So what do the people get? An online account with founder status, a three-D printed dome model keychain, a rear view mirror hanger, a window decal, a poster. The middle tier adds a signed book that goes along with this codebase, the campaign, and the whole dome paradigm. The high tier gets help idealizing and building digitally with me: game-plan forming for your own dome realization. For future pad owners, dome collectors, and anybody gathering possibilities for later. Those are the proposed categories. The campaign will set the actual tiers and delivery scope.

chapters.title: Bring your own dome
chapters.promise: Keep the value of the home you improve.
chapters.narration: A hotel sells you a night. A short let sells you a fortnight. A lease sells you a year and then charges you to leave early. And a rental home is somebody handing you a money shredder at your convenience, for use on your own stash. One of those sells you the thing most people actually want, which is to live somewhere for a while without handing over the value of everything they do to the place while they are there. Bring your own home. Pay the host for the ground and the services. Improve your house as much as you like, because it is your house, and take every bit of that with you when you go. The source, the model inputs and the experiments should be open. Actual open source, not the kind where the word is doing marketing. The drawings, the prices and the things that fail should all be available to check. Nothing in this film was asserted. Every pad and every dome was drawn by the tool that designs them. Every figure was computed by the model underneath it, and the numbers that argue against this idea are in here with the ones that argue for it. Come and check them.

chapters.title: One person who can carry it further
chapters.promise: Send this to someone who should see it.
chapters.narration: And one last thing, said plainly. If this campaign does not fund, my plan and my work are the same. I am building this whether it takes one year or ten. What a donation changes is the speed, and whether the drawings reach anybody else on the way. If any of this was worth your time, send it to one person who can carry it further than I can. That is the whole ask. One share from somebody with reach does more for this than a month of me in a field with a chainsaw.

chapters.title: Follow the experiments
chapters.promise: Follow the experiments.
chapters.narration: Everything is documented, including the parts that failed. Instagram, Donovan Zeanah. Facebook dot com slash zeanah. TikTok, short circuiter five. GitHub dot com slash d k zeanah. Zeanah Lab dot com and a Kickstarter for Frankendome are both coming soon.

title: Bring Your Own Dome (polished)
note: Bring Your Own Dome as a considered presentation: the camera drifts in slowly, the pace is generous, nothing is laid over the frame, and no character appears. The control for the snarky cut -- one script, two registers.
family_note: a style variant of the same script

chapters.title: A home you keep
chapters.promise: BRING YOUR OWN DOME
chapters.narration: Bring your own dome. Build a home. Improve it. Take it with you.

chapters.title: An RV park, for houses
chapters.promise: Serviced pads. You bring the home.
chapters.narration: Think of it as a fancier trailer park. Or maybe better: a stationary RV park, where the thing you park is a house you built and can take apart again.

chapters.title: Why would someone host a dome?
chapters.promise: Passive income, without the rental maintenance.
chapters.narration: So why would people want to host these things? Passive income. Income from land, without the infrastructural maintenance that comes with rental homes. We know the pains of landlords. We know the pains of tenants. I want to bridge the two of them, so that both sides love the arrangement, and each other. That is the dream, anyway.

chapters.title: The pad, and the house that lands on it
chapters.promise: A landowner builds the pad. A dome owner plugs in.
chapters.narration: A landowner builds a circular service pad. A dome owner arrives with their home, sets it down on the pad, and plugs in.

chapters.title: Two people, two colours, one line
chapters.promise: Amber is the pad. Cyan is the house.
chapters.narration: Everything you are about to see is drawn by the Dome Creator's own renderer, and every number comes off the same model the tool uses. There are two people in this network and they want opposite things, so this film keeps them in different colours the whole way through. Amber is the pad host: the deck, the trench, the pedestal, the meter. Cyan is the dome owner: the house, and everything they ever do to it. The single most important thing about that line is that it never moves. The host never owns a building somebody else is living in, and the tenant never pays rent on something that will never be theirs. Which means both sides keep control of their own half. Fewer things to argue about, because there are fewer things held in common. And an easy goodbye, which is worth more than people think: if it is not working, the dome leaves, and the pad is exactly as it was.

chapters.title: A side thought
chapters.promise: Domes make good climate-controlled storage.
chapters.narration: A sidenote. I think domes make great air-conditioned storage. A compact shell leans on the same efficient heating and cooling principles the houses do, and the pad underneath it is already there. It would need its own performance and cost check, and it is not the business this film is about. But housing is not the only thing the same kit of parts can do.

chapters.title: The reserved spot
chapters.promise: Utilities in the centre. Choices around them.
chapters.narration: Pads have their service in the middle. That is the spot every dome builder knows is reserved for the utility station. It is not the only way to do it. It is the only way I will do it. Everything in the dome is reachable from a service point at the centre, and that is what makes the space movable. The partitioning can change without the plumbing having to move with it.

chapters.title: Your life changes. The rooms can too.
chapters.promise: Bedroom, then office, then bedroom again.
chapters.narration: Split a large bedroom to make an office. Three years later you retire, stop needing the office, and open the bedroom back up. I live in a trailer. Four bedrooms, a living room, a den, an office, two bathrooms, a kitchen and a dining area. We have all the allotments of a domicile. But much of that space could be reallocated more efficiently, because the way we need it changed over time. I was gone for six years. I came back. Three people became four, and eventually the same house will be too much for one person. The dome does not have that problem. The shell stays. The room plan can change.

chapters.title: Watch one get built
chapters.promise: Grade, deck, rim, services.
chapters.narration: Change a number in the model and every figure after it moves, because the film reads the table rather than repeating it. So what is a pad? Watch one get built. Grade the ground. Then a deck: gravel, concrete or timber, whatever the host wants to pay for. Then an acceptor rim around the edge. That rim is the part a dome latches to, and it is the reason this is a pad rather than a patio.

chapters.title: Whatever the host wants to pay for
chapters.promise: Gravel, concrete, timber.
chapters.narration: The deck is most of what a pad costs, and it is priced by area, so it is priced by diameter squared. Gravel is the cheapest surface that is still a floor. Concrete is the slab a contractor pours. Timber is the deck a carpenter builds. Everything else on the pad is roughly fixed: the hookups, the permits, and the road that had to reach the site in the first place.

chapters.title: One pad. More than one dome size.
chapters.promise: An iris, with leaves you can watch move.
chapters.narration: That rim is not a fixed ring. It is an iris, on a track, with leaves that open and close like a camera aperture. Watch the contact points move inward, then outward. So one pad takes a twenty foot dome or a forty foot one without being rebuilt. That is the whole reason a host can serve a range of domes with a single piece of hardware. The mechanism is a development concept, and it belongs in the upgrade column.

chapters.title: The deluxe version
chapters.promise: A foundation that turns the house to face what you want.
chapters.narration: Then there is the top-line version: a rotating foundation, with the tracking built into it. This is the expensive one. And honestly, it is just freaking cool. Imagine some days I want the window looking out on the street or the highway. Some days I have someone over, and I want it facing the back corner of the lot instead, where the fence is high. Imagine I have no solar panels at all. Maybe I like the sun in my face in the morning. Maybe I get tired of that and want the opposite, so I face away from it entirely. I imagine there is a lot to be gained from a rotational house in that manner, and more again with panels covering certain parts of the shell asymmetrically. But the bearing, the drive and the rotating utility connections all need their own design. This is future deluxe hardware, at deluxe pricing.

chapters.title: The wedge dome's service channels
chapters.promise: Up the centre. Along the shell. Out of the way.
chapters.narration: Here is the wedge build with its points facing outward. The paired members leave a channel along every seam, and those seams connect around the whole shell. The same orientation gives a panel area with a lip, so a slanted face panel can seat against it and stop where it should.

chapters.title: A place for the panels to seat
chapters.promise: The outward wedge leaves a tapered opening.
chapters.narration: That is the direction I want to take the frame: removable panels, accessible channels, and attachments that can be improved without throwing the skeleton away.

chapters.title: Veins along the outside skin
chapters.promise: From the centre, up, and then out.
chapters.narration: Power, water and drain arrive in the centre. Centre, not edge. From there the runs can go upwards, and then out and into the edge areas, almost like veins along the outside skin of the dome. Latched in place. Out of the way, accessible, and semi-permanent. Which means my dome is now looking like a Brainiac build. That fits, considering the first model I called the Frankendome, a conglomerate of strut types. Apparently I have a theme.

chapters.title: The pad is the floor
chapters.promise: No foundation. No slab. Nothing left behind.
chapters.narration: The dome that lands here puts its floor on the pad. So the services have to come up inside the footprint, or they cross the doorway. A utility column if the host wants one: toilet, sink, shower head, outlets, and a meter pedestal at the rim. The dome that arrives does not bring a foundation, because it does not need one. The pad is the floor. The deck it lands on is the deck it lives on. Bringing the carpet is up to the dome owner. I would. I love carpet. Some people want a garage-shop floor through the whole house. I have seen it. It works. When the owner leaves, the pad is exactly as it was. No slab to break out, no footing to dig up, no permit pulled for a structure that will be gone in a year. We already see dome rentals. They are cheaper to build than a house, and most glamping domes are, let us be honest, glorified tents. I do not think their value ever gets realized by renting them out a weekend at a time. But if a person owned their glorified tent and rented the space to put it on instead, now we are talking. Now both sides get something, and both sides are geared for a long-term exchange of service. Renting a house has never been a way forward for me. Buy-here-pay-here anything is for people with no choice but to be used as pawns by the banking system. A dome is the way out. It is my way out, at the very least. If I can bring people along with me, my job here is done.

chapters.title: The pad catalogue
chapters.promise: Sizes are not invented. They are rounded up.
chapters.narration: Pads come in sizes, and the sizes are not invented. Every design the Dome Creator ships has a foundation diameter, and the tool computes it from its own geometry. Round each one up to the next four feet and you have the pad catalog. Four foot steps, because decking and ring stock come in even lengths, and because the second pad a host builds wants the first one's cut list. Add a bigger dome to the tool, and a bigger pad size appears here on the next run. Nobody edits a list.

chapters.title: What the host actually owns
chapters.promise: A deck, a rim, three pipes and a conduit.
chapters.narration: Look at what the host owns here, because it is a short list. A deck, a rim, three pipes and a conduit, a pedestal with a meter in it, maybe a ring and a column. And it does not have to be poured. There is no kitchen to replace. No sofa to re-upholster. No flooring to pull up because a ten-inch dog lived on it. The host asset is a piece of civil engineering, and the thing most likely to damage it is weather.

chapters.title: Start with the cheapest working version
chapters.promise: A small serviced deck, before the deluxe extras.
chapters.narration: The cheapest version that is still a service pad is a frame deck on pre-cast blocks, with one power panel and a water manifold in the middle of four domes, instead of a pedestal and a trench for each. Nothing excavated, nothing poured. Here is the build cost, line by line, for the smallest pad that takes a real house. Note the two lines that are usually missing from a pitch like this. Site infrastructure: something had to bring a road, a water main and a service drop to this spot, and that cost is real whether or not you count it. And permits. That puts this version above my ten thousand dollar target. It tells me where the design work has to go. It does not justify pretending the difference is gone.

chapters.title: What would a ten-thousand-dollar pad return?
chapters.promise: The target, tested at three proposed rents.
chapters.narration: If I can make pads at or around a ten thousand dollar build-out, with the water and electrical tie-ins included, it could immediately be rented to a dome owner for what? Five hundred, a thousand, fifteen hundred a month. At the high end it pays itself back inside a year, no contest. And there is nothing there to degrade to begin with, so it is easily a ten-year-plus infrastructural commodity. On the income side the lease is most of it. The utility margin is a cent or two a unit, and that is payment for metering and paperwork rather than a second rent. Here it comes to about ten dollars a month. And payback is on net, after management, tax and insurance. Payback on gross is a brochure number.

chapters.title: Below the line and above it
chapters.promise: The host's money is in the ground. The tenant's goes with them.
chapters.narration: Two people, one pad, and a line between them that does not move. Below the line is the host's money, and it is in the ground. Above the line is the tenant's money, and it is a drive away with them. That is the arrangement, and it is the opposite of every other way people rent somewhere to live. A landlord's money is in the walls the tenant is living between. That is where the conflict comes from, every time.

chapters.title: The comparison a host actually makes
chapters.promise: Fewer recurring household costs.
chapters.narration: The honest comparison for a landowner is not against nothing. It is against furnishing a place and letting it out, which is what most people with a spare building actually do. So both columns carry the same management, the same tax, the same insurance. The short-let scenario of renting by the building then adds cleaning at every turnover, a damage reserve, a platform fee and a renovation cycle. Several times the pad host's yearly bill, forever. A dome pad is a truly passive income asset.

chapters.title: The work I want to do
chapters.promise: Design the pads. Make the next site repeatable.
chapters.narration: My eventual business, the role I will inevitably fill, is pad design and initializing for hosts. Unique feature sets can go here. Floor heating. Built-in water storage. Built-in deep-freeze storage. Rotation and sun tracking. A concrete shop floor, ready to work on. And eventually the computer and smart-system brains, which is for later. The first job is to make the simple version work well enough that another host can build it from a clear plan.

chapters.title: Now show the deluxe price
chapters.promise: Rotation, adjustable iris, utility column, and solar.
chapters.narration: And now the figure that does not help us. A loaded pad, rotating, plumbed, carrying an array, costs more upfront than a bare pad with a furnished let on it. On day one, the short-let house rental wins. The pad host case was never that it is cheaper to start. It is that none of their yearly bill is where a building somebody else is living in.

chapters.title: The part you can leave to the site
chapters.promise: The same home. A different arrangement underneath.
chapters.narration: Now the tenant side, and it starts underground. On the left, the design as the Dome Creator ships it, standing on its own foundation. On the right, the same design on a pad, with that foundation taken out from under it, because the pad is already there. Same house. The difference is the ground, and the ground is the one part of a building you can never take with you when you go.

chapters.title: What a stay costs
chapters.promise: One model. Utilities included on every line.
chapters.narration: Here is the comparison a person actually makes, priced on one basis, so it is a fair one. Every line carries power and water, because two of them include it in the nightly rate, and quietly dropping it from the other two would rig the result. The dome line carries the two costs an ownership pitch usually hides: upkeep, and the return the money would have made if it were not sitting in a house. And it is worth less the day after you buy it, so a secondhand haircut comes off on day one. Pay to build your dream home and only you value every personal choice at the full price you paid. So fifteen percent comes off that just to start the negotiation. Even carrying all of that, a year in your own dome on a pad costs less than a year in the cheapest thing you could rent. And at the end of it you still own a house.

chapters.title: Too long to be a guest
chapters.promise: Too uncertain to sign for a year.
chapters.narration: So how long does the stay have to be? Run those same four options at every length, and find the month the dome stops being the expensive answer. Nobody should buy a house to stay somewhere for a month. Under that line a short let is the right answer, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. Past it, the gap opens and never closes. Most people fit in the categories this is aimed at: too long to be a guest, too uncertain to sign for a year. That is the part of the market neither a hotel nor a twelve month lease has ever served.

chapters.title: What this would have meant to me
chapters.promise: A stable home before the next big step.
chapters.narration: When I was nineteen I was able to borrow five grand against my name, for college. I blew that, joined the military, and now at thirty-two I am back for revenge. Constructive revenge, apparently involving domes. I did not fail out because I was stupid. I had no overarching support, I was not stable in my living situations, and I could not focus on the thing that mattered in that time: school. It cost me greatly. Tremendously, if you ask me. What a dome would have done for my eighteen-year-old self would have been revolutionary. That is how I am designing this, and going forward.

chapters.title: Built with the little guy in mind
chapters.promise: Students. Single parents. New families.
chapters.narration: I think college-aged students would get three times the investment out of a dome system than out of a squandered semester. A realistic five thousand dollar dome home is doable, especially when you rely on the pad for the essentials. The trailer model of the dome world, so to speak. Rich people will find their own way to have what they want without me. The small people, that is who I can impact. Single mothers. The economically vulnerable. Starting families. Bachelors. My mother was a poor single parent. She worked so much that I went to the before-school program and the after-school program on the same day. I wish she had had a stable, economical home system that worked for her and made sense. I would love to be so successful that I can give away domes. Maybe by then I am making dome furniture too. That is an ambition. The first step is a home people can afford to start with and improve.

chapters.title: Semi-nomadic
chapters.promise: Move when it is worth the effort.
chapters.narration: The word that describes the whole idea is semi-nomadic. Not a caravan you tow away on a whim. A house that comes apart: two days at the quick end, two weeks for something large or heavily layered. That is a real burst of effort, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But it is a burst, not a condition. You spend it when a move is worth it, and the rest of the time you are simply living in a house. Off one pad and onto another. A different park, a different city, a different state. No lease broken, no deposit argued over, no walkthrough with somebody's clipboard. Nothing left behind, and every improvement the owner has ever made goes with them. The money they spent is still theirs, standing on the next pad.

chapters.title: The same design, scaled
chapters.promise: Part counts stay fixed. Materials grow with the house.
chapters.narration: Take one design and move a single slider: the radius. Everything else is held exactly where it was. Twenty feet across, thirty-three feet across, fifty-two feet across. Two hundred and ninety-five square feet up to two thousand and ninety-six. And the part list on the bench in front of you never changes. The counts are identical across all three. The same struts, the same hubs, the same panels. And the hub bill is identical to the same dollars at twenty feet as it is at fifty-two. What does move is the stick and the skin, because those are priced by the meter and the square meter. Seven times the floor off the same list of parts. The hardware is a range of sizes, shipped with two sizes up in mind as the base level. That is what makes one good hardware set worth paying for: it is the part of the house that does not change when the house does, so it is the part you buy once and keep.

chapters.title: Buy for the next two steps
chapters.promise: Keep the hardware. Collect the longer members.
chapters.narration: Pads come in sizes, and so does the hardware. Start with the base model and size it two steps ahead. For my wedge system the plan is to start with a six foot long member, go to ten feet, then twelve: about twelve hundred square feet at that final target size. Any bigger, and we start upping the dome frequency. Sinking capital into the hardware majority is the advantage, because that is the part that remains and gets reused when a bigger dome is wanted. The longer members get collected gradually, on the way. That is why I would put money into a good hardware set: it should remain useful across a planned range of builds.

chapters.title: A lesson from the Arctic
chapters.promise: Layers under a removable weather shell.
chapters.narration: Some of my own practices make their way into these domes. I stood lookout outside the skin of a ship in the Arctic Circle, for hours at a time, over months. There is exactly one way to stay warm out there: layers on layers on layers, and then a wind-breaking, watertight suit over all of it. You end up looking like the Michelin man. You also stay alive. It was not that bad. A dome with a removable shell can work the same way. Lift the shell, add a quilted layer, put the shell back over it. Quilted recycled fabric is one of the largest waste streams there is.

chapters.title: Improve it over time
chapters.promise: The number keeps going up for as long as you own it.
chapters.narration: Which means our value stops being a number somebody decided on the day the house was built. The R-value is not a static figure. It can keep going up for as long as you own the house: better at heating and better at cooling, year after year, because you added the layer that was worth adding that year. Two honest limits. Seven layers is a good wall, not a code-beating one. And this prices conduction only. It does not price the windbreak, and the windbreak is what makes layers work. That is the shell's job, and it is the part of the Arctic argument this model cannot check.

chapters.title: How much shell can carry solar?
chapters.promise: One side. Top half. Whole shell.
chapters.narration: A pad on a rotating base can aim whatever is standing on it. The dome in this chapter is a ten foot radius shell, the medium two-person size, because kilowatt hours a month mean nothing without the dome they came off. Three ways to clad it. One side, so the pad turns that side to the sun. The top half, with a metal skirt below it, where the skirt is the rain catchment as well as the weather edge. Or the whole shell, which makes the most power and gives you the least reason to turn anything, because something is always facing the sun. Single axis tracking adds about a quarter over a fixed array, and on this dome that is several hundred kilowatt hours a month.

chapters.title: The size sets a limit
chapters.promise: Capacity from panel area. Output depends on the site.
chapters.narration: Here are the relative capacities, using the measured face area and the model's declared panel density. The limit is the shell area: at this size the layouts run from about five to ten kilowatts of nameplate capacity, and a larger shell has more area to work with. But here is the number that first made this model wrong. A dome shell carries far more panel than a household inside it consumes. Several times more. The first version of this model valued every generated kilowatt hour at the retail price, which quietly assumed the tenant was buying power they would never have bought. So it does not any more. What displaces the tenant's own draw is worth retail. Everything past it is worth export, which is about a third of that. Correcting it took this pad's solar income down by well over half. The ring is still worth fitting. But the real case for cladding a dome in cells is a park that can sell the surplus, not a tenant who cannot use it.

chapters.title: What a site can share
chapters.promise: A bathhouse. A utility core. A choice of services.
chapters.narration: Some of this can be shared, and that changes what a dome has to be. A bathhouse on the site means a dome owner can skip plumbing entirely, which is the single most expensive and most regulated thing in a small dwelling. Or the host fits the utility column on the pad, once, for every tenant who ever parks there. Either way it is bought once by the person who owns it, and used by everyone who comes and goes. And note what a host is not obliged to do. Reselling power and water with a margin is one option, not the model. A host may simply pass the meter through. What a host is really competing on is the array of things a site offers, and the price they can ask follows from that.

chapters.title: Why a network matters
chapters.promise: More places to go. More people who can use the system.
chapters.narration: The closest thing that exists is an RV park, and the comparison is worth making carefully. An RV park turns over in nights and weeks. A dome park turns over in seasons and years, because taking a dome down is a job rather than a decision. Same shape of arrangement, much longer clock. One host with one pad is a favor. What makes this worth building is the second host, and the third, and the four hundredth. For the dome owner, a network means choice: price, location, services, and the freedom to leave a bad host by driving away from them. For the pad host, it means a tenant pool that is not limited to whoever happens to be in town, and it means the dome has a resale market, which is the one assumption in this film doing the most work. A house you can sell is an asset. A house nobody will buy is a very expensive tent.

chapters.title: Small scale. Small risk.
chapters.promise: Prove a small site, then make it repeatable.
chapters.narration: The goal is a hundred thousand dollars. I think that is a modest number to strive for, and it is modest because the expensive parts are already mine: the land, and somewhere to work. What the money builds is one to three pads on that land, as a test group, and the pad architecture itself made repeatable, the way RV hookups are repeatable, so the second site is a cut list rather than an invention. Most of it goes into modular design and the means to do it. A full woodworking and metalworking shop. CNC plasma torches, three-D printers, a mill, casting materials, a laser, a router: a lab for panelizing the frame and skeleton I already have realized. One to three dome designs that actually suit this, built and measured. Then the web app and its hosting and promotion. Real advertising on every platform I can reach, because I want this idea to spread like the flu rather than sit in a repository. And a camera, because all of it gets published as it is made. What the campaign does not buy is the tracking foundation. A pad that turns to follow the sun is a fine thing to own and I intend to build one, but it is whimsy on the first site, and I am not spending anyone else's money on it.

chapters.title: What supporters get
chapters.promise: Founder status. A signed book. Help shaping your own build.
chapters.narration: So what do the people get? An online account with founder status, a three-D printed dome model keychain, a rear view mirror hanger, a window decal, a poster. The middle tier adds a signed book that goes along with this codebase, the campaign, and the whole dome paradigm. The high tier gets help idealizing and building digitally with me: game-plan forming for your own dome realization. For future pad owners, dome collectors, and anybody gathering possibilities for later. Those are the proposed categories. The campaign will set the actual tiers and delivery scope.

chapters.title: Bring your own dome
chapters.promise: Keep the value of the home you improve.
chapters.narration: A hotel sells you a night. A short let sells you a fortnight. A lease sells you a year and then charges you to leave early. And a rental home is somebody handing you a money shredder at your convenience, for use on your own stash. One of those sells you the thing most people actually want, which is to live somewhere for a while without handing over the value of everything they do to the place while they are there. Bring your own home. Pay the host for the ground and the services. Improve your house as much as you like, because it is your house, and take every bit of that with you when you go. The source, the model inputs and the experiments should be open. Actual open source, not the kind where the word is doing marketing. The drawings, the prices and the things that fail should all be available to check. Nothing in this film was asserted. Every pad and every dome was drawn by the tool that designs them. Every figure was computed by the model underneath it, and the numbers that argue against this idea are in here with the ones that argue for it. Come and check them.

chapters.title: One person who can carry it further
chapters.promise: Send this to someone who should see it.
chapters.narration: And one last thing, said plainly. If this campaign does not fund, my plan and my work are the same. I am building this whether it takes one year or ten. What a donation changes is the speed, and whether the drawings reach anybody else on the way. If any of this was worth your time, send it to one person who can carry it further than I can. That is the whole ask. One share from somebody with reach does more for this than a month of me in a field with a chainsaw.
